declarations.name: ZONE_BODY_SENSATIONS
declarations.source:
var ZONE_BODY_SENSATIONS = [
    // ===== HEAD =====
    {
      id: 'head_foggy',
      sensation: 'foggy head, hard to think clearly',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'cognitive',
      zoneIndicator: 'blue',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your head feels like it is full of clouds. It is hard to remember what you were just doing.',
        middle: 'Your thinking feels slow and unclear, like trying to see through fog. Words and ideas come more slowly than usual.',
        high: 'Cognitive processing feels sluggish and unfocused, often accompanied by reduced verbal fluency. Mental fatigue dominates attention.'
      },
      forWho: 'depressed, exhausted, post-illness, dissociating, dehydrated, autistic post-overload',
      whatItMeans: 'Brain fog often signals reduced cerebral blood flow, fatigue, dehydration, or post-stress recovery. It is a sign the body is asking for rest or fuel.',
      whatToDo: 'Hydrate, eat a small protein snack, and try a 2-minute movement break. If it persists, lower the cognitive demand and switch to a simpler task.',
      cautions: 'Fog that lasts for days with headache, confusion, or fever warrants medical evaluation.',
      research: 'Barrett, L. F. (2017) body-budget framework; Mahler, K. (2019) interoception curriculum.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_dizzy',
      sensation: 'room feels like it is spinning or tilting',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'vestibular',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'The room feels like it is moving even when you are still. You might want to sit down.',
        middle: 'You feel off-balance like you stood up too fast or got off a spinning ride. The world tilts a little.',
        high: 'Vestibular disequilibrium produces a perception of motion that is not occurring. It can accompany anxiety, dehydration, or inner-ear disturbance.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, panic-prone, dehydrated, low blood sugar, postural',
      whatItMeans: 'Dizziness during stress often reflects hyperventilation and reduced CO2, which constricts blood vessels in the brain. It also signals dehydration or low fuel.',
      whatToDo: 'Sit or lie down, slow your breath (inhale 4, exhale 6), and sip water. Place a hand on a solid surface to re-anchor balance.',
      cautions: 'Sudden severe dizziness with vision loss, slurred speech, or one-sided weakness needs emergency care.',
      research: 'Khalsa, S. (2018) interoception and anxiety; Craig, A. D. (2009) interoceptive cortex.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_light',
      sensation: 'head feels light or floaty',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'vestibular',
      zoneIndicator: 'ambiguous',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your head feels like a balloon. It is not bad, but it is a different feeling.',
        middle: 'Your head feels weightless or floaty, like you are just slightly outside your body.',
        high: 'A sense of cranial weightlessness can signal early hyperventilation, blood-sugar shift, or a dissociative response to overwhelm.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, dissociating, hungry, post-stress',
      whatItMeans: 'Lightness in the head often reflects rapid breathing or blood-sugar dips. It can also be a mild dissociation signal in trauma-affected students.',
      whatToDo: 'Ground through your feet, name 3 things you can see, and take 3 slow exhales. Eat a small carbohydrate if it has been more than 3 hours since you ate.',
      cautions: 'Floaty sensations with fainting, confusion, or chest pain need medical review.',
      research: 'Porges, S. (2011) polyvagal theory; Garfinkel, S. (2015) interoceptive accuracy.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_heavy',
      sensation: 'head feels heavy like a bowling ball',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'blue',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your head feels really heavy. It is hard to hold it up.',
        middle: 'Your head feels weighted, like you want to rest it on your hand or a pillow.',
        high: 'A sense of cranial heaviness often signals fatigue, low arousal, or the postural shift of sadness and shutdown.'
      },
      forWho: 'depressed, exhausted, grieving, sick',
      whatItMeans: 'Heavy head signals low arousal and reduced muscle activation in the neck and upper back. The body is asking for rest.',
      whatToDo: 'Allow a short rest with head supported, then try gentle neck rolls and a brief walk. Sunlight and water often help.',
      cautions: 'Persistent heaviness with nausea, vision change, or one-sided weakness needs medical attention.',
      research: 'Mahler, K. (2019) interoception in classrooms; Barrett, L. F. (2017) allostasis.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_pressure',
      sensation: 'pressure or band-like tightness around the head',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'It feels like a tight headband is squeezing your head.',
        middle: 'You feel a band of pressure around your forehead or temples. It usually means stress is building.',
        high: 'Tension-type headache pattern often signals sustained sympathetic activation, screen strain, or dehydration.'
      },
      forWho: 'stressed, anxious, screen-fatigued, dehydrated',
      whatItMeans: 'Head pressure usually reflects scalp and neck muscle tension plus reduced hydration. It is a yellow-zone early warning.',
      whatToDo: 'Look 20 feet away for 20 seconds, roll your shoulders, sip water, and unclench your jaw.',
      cautions: 'Sudden severe headache (worst of life), vision change, or confusion needs emergency care.',
      research: 'IHS Classification of Headache Disorders; Mahler interoception curriculum.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_throbbing',
      sensation: 'throbbing or pulsing in head',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'cardiac',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 4,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your head hurts and you can feel it thumping like a heartbeat.',
        middle: 'You feel a pulsing pain in your head, often on one side. It can come with light or sound sensitivity.',
        high: 'Pulsatile cephalgia, often vascular, may reflect migraine, dehydration, or high blood pressure during acute stress.'
      },
      forWho: 'migraine-prone, dehydrated, hormonal, high-stress',
      whatItMeans: 'Throbbing reflects blood-vessel pulsation in the head, often during migraine onset or intense stress.',
      whatToDo: 'Move to a dim quiet space, hydrate, and use any prescribed migraine plan. Cold cloth on forehead can help.',
      cautions: 'Sudden severe throbbing with vomiting, stiff neck, or vision loss needs emergency care.',
      research: 'American Migraine Foundation clinical guidelines; Garfinkel interoception research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_scalp_tingle',
      sensation: 'scalp tingling or prickling',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'ambiguous',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your scalp feels like little bubbles or tingles.',
        middle: 'You feel a tingly or prickly sensation across your scalp, sometimes pleasant, sometimes alarming.',
        high: 'Scalp paresthesia can accompany stress, sensory engagement (ASMR), or shifts in autonomic tone.'
      },
      forWho: 'anyone; common in ASMR-sensitive students and during emotional moments',
      whatItMeans: 'Tingling is often a sensory shift in autonomic tone. Pleasant tingling is generally safe; uncomfortable tingling with anxiety may signal hyperventilation.',
      whatToDo: 'Notice without judging. If it accompanies fast breathing, slow your exhale.',
      cautions: 'Persistent numbness or one-sided scalp sensation change needs medical review.',
      research: 'Poerio, G. L. (2018) ASMR autonomic response; Khalsa interoception studies.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_ear_ringing',
      sensation: 'ringing or high-pitched sound in ears',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'You hear a buzzing or ringing sound that no one else hears.',
        middle: 'You hear a high-pitched ring or hiss inside your ears, often when it is quiet or you are stressed.',
        high: 'Tinnitus can intensify during stress, fatigue, or after loud sound exposure. It is often benign but worth tracking.'
      },
      forWho: 'stressed, fatigued, post-loud-event, sensory-sensitive',
      whatItMeans: 'Stress-related tinnitus reflects amplified auditory processing during sympathetic activation. Background noise often masks it.',
      whatToDo: 'Add gentle background sound (fan, soft music), hydrate, and lower acute stress. Note triggers for the school nurse.',
      cautions: 'Sudden one-sided ringing with hearing loss or vertigo needs prompt medical care.',
      research: 'American Tinnitus Association clinical guidance; ASHA interoception-audiology overlap.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_eye_strain',
      sensation: 'eye strain or burning eyes',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your eyes feel tired and a little sore.',
        middle: 'Your eyes feel tight, dry, or burning, especially after screens or close work.',
        high: 'Digital eye strain reflects reduced blink rate and sustained ciliary muscle accommodation during screen use.'
      },
      forWho: 'screen-using, reading-fatigued, dehydrated',
      whatItMeans: 'Eye strain usually signals visual fatigue from sustained near-work. It often coincides with rising overall tension.',
      whatToDo: 'Use 20-20-20 (every 20 min, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds). Blink intentionally and hydrate.',
      cautions: 'Sudden vision changes, double vision, or eye pain needs medical review.',
      research: 'American Academy of Ophthalmology screen guidelines.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_eye_watering',
      sensation: 'eyes watering or tearing without crying',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'ambiguous',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your eyes get watery even though you are not crying.',
        middle: 'Your eyes well up unexpectedly, sometimes with emotion, sometimes with strain or allergies.',
        high: 'Lacrimation can reflect emotional surfacing, allergens, dryness, or vagal activity.'
      },
      forWho: 'emotional, allergic, dry-eye prone',
      whatItMeans: 'Watery eyes can be a quiet emotional signal before conscious feelings arrive, or simply a reflex to dryness.',
      whatToDo: 'Notice gently. If it links to emotion, name what you might be feeling without forcing it.',
      cautions: 'One-sided redness with pain needs medical evaluation.',
      research: 'Vingerhoets, A. (2013) crying psychology; Porges polyvagal theory.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_vision_tunnel',
      sensation: 'vision narrows or tunnels',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 4,
      description: {
        elementary: 'It feels like you are looking through a small tube.',
        middle: 'Your side vision dims and you only see straight ahead, like a tunnel forming.',
        high: 'Peripheral vision narrowing during acute stress reflects sympathetic dominance and adrenergic vascular shifts.'
      },
      forWho: 'panic, high-stress, pre-faint, trauma-activated',
      whatItMeans: 'Tunnel vision signals strong fight-or-flight activation or near-faint. The body is funneling resources to threat detection.',
      whatToDo: 'Sit down immediately, slow your exhale, and look around the room naming objects to expand visual field.',
      cautions: 'Sudden vision loss, severe headache, or one-sided weakness needs emergency care.',
      research: 'Porges polyvagal theory; van der Kolk, B. (2014) trauma physiology.'
    },
    {
      id: 'head_visual_flicker',
      sensation: 'visual flickering or zigzag lights',
      bodyRegion: 'head',
      system: 'sensory',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'You see flashing or zigzag shapes that are not really there.',
        middle: 'You see shimmering lights, zigzags, or blind spots, often before a headache.',
        high: 'Visual aura, often migraine-related, reflects cortical spreading depression in occipital cortex.'
      },
      forWho: 'migraine-prone, post-strobe-exposure, fatigued',
      whatItMeans: 'Visual aura is often the brain announcing a migraine 15 to 60 minutes ahead. It is a warning, not a danger by itself.',
      whatToDo: 'Move to dim quiet space, hydrate, and start any prescribed migraine plan. Tell a trusted adult.',
      cautions: 'First-ever aura, aura without resolution, or aura with weakness needs medical review.',
      research: 'American Migraine Foundation; Hadjikhani, N. (2001) cortical spreading depression.'
    },
    // ===== FACE =====
    {
      id: 'face_hot',
      sensation: 'face feels hot or burning',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'skin',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your cheeks feel really warm, like you just ran around.',
        middle: 'Your face feels hot and you might look red, especially when embarrassed or angry.',
        high: 'Facial flushing reflects vasodilation often driven by emotion (anger, shame, embarrassment) or exertion.'
      },
      forWho: 'embarrassed, angry, anxious, post-exercise',
      whatItMeans: 'Heat in the face signals strong emotional activation, often anger, shame, or embarrassment. It is information, not a problem.',
      whatToDo: 'Name the feeling silently, take a slow breath, and let the heat pass without fighting it. A cool drink can help.',
      cautions: 'Persistent flushing with itching or breathing trouble may signal allergy and needs medical care.',
      research: 'Drummond, P. (2013) facial blushing physiology; Keltner emotion research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_pale',
      sensation: 'face feels cold or pale',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'skin',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 4,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your face feels cold and might look white.',
        middle: 'The blood drains from your face and you feel cold or clammy. It often comes with fear or shock.',
        high: 'Facial pallor reflects sympathetic vasoconstriction redirecting blood to large muscles during acute threat or pre-syncope.'
      },
      forWho: 'fearful, shocked, pre-faint, traumatized',
      whatItMeans: 'Pale cold face often signals strong fight-flight or pre-faint response. The body is rerouting blood to survival systems.',
      whatToDo: 'Sit or lie down, raise feet slightly if pre-faint, and breathe slowly. Tell a trusted adult.',
      cautions: 'Pale face with chest pain, confusion, or fainting needs emergency care.',
      research: 'Porges polyvagal theory; cardiology pre-syncope guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_jaw_tight',
      sensation: 'jaw clenched or tight',
      bodyRegion: 'jaw',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your teeth feel like they are pressing together hard.',
        middle: 'Your jaw is tight and your teeth might be clenched without you noticing.',
        high: 'Masseter and temporalis hyperactivity reflects sympathetic tone and is a leading bruxism indicator.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, focused-on-difficult-task, asleep-stressed, ADHD',
      whatItMeans: 'A clenched jaw is one of the body\'s most common stress holding spots. Many students do not notice it until pain develops.',
      whatToDo: 'Drop your jaw slightly with tongue resting behind front teeth, hum a low note, or yawn intentionally.',
      cautions: 'Jaw pain with locking, clicking, or headache for weeks needs dental review.',
      research: 'AAOP TMD guidelines; Mahler interoception body-mapping.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_jaw_soft',
      sensation: 'jaw soft and relaxed',
      bodyRegion: 'jaw',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'green',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your jaw feels easy and loose.',
        middle: 'Your teeth are slightly apart, your tongue rests easy, and your jaw feels open.',
        high: 'A soft jaw reflects parasympathetic balance and is a marker of regulated state.'
      },
      forWho: 'regulated, calm, post-co-regulation',
      whatItMeans: 'A loose jaw is a quiet sign your nervous system is settled. Notice and savor it.',
      whatToDo: 'Notice the relaxation and try to recall what helped you get here. Use it as a reference for future regulation.',
      cautions: 'No cautions for relaxation.',
      research: 'Porges polyvagal safe-and-social state; Mahler interoception.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_eye_twitch',
      sensation: 'eyelid twitching',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your eyelid jumps a little on its own.',
        middle: 'A small muscle in your eyelid flickers without you choosing it.',
        high: 'Myokymia of the orbicularis oculi often reflects fatigue, caffeine, stress, or dehydration.'
      },
      forWho: 'tired, caffeinated, stressed, screen-fatigued',
      whatItMeans: 'Eye twitching is a benign signal that your nervous system is overtaxed. It usually resolves with rest and hydration.',
      whatToDo: 'Sleep more, reduce caffeine, hydrate, and rest your eyes. It usually passes within days.',
      cautions: 'Twitching that spreads to the face or lasts weeks needs medical review.',
      research: 'AAO eyelid myokymia overview.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_mouth_dry',
      sensation: 'mouth feels dry or sticky',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'GI',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your mouth feels dry and your tongue is sticky.',
        middle: 'Your mouth dries up before you speak in front of people or during a test.',
        high: 'Stress-related xerostomia reflects sympathetic suppression of salivary flow.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious-before-performance, dehydrated, medicated',
      whatItMeans: 'A dry mouth is a fight-flight signal. Saliva production drops when the body prioritizes survival over digestion.',
      whatToDo: 'Sip water, press tongue to roof of mouth and release, or chew sugar-free gum to stimulate saliva.',
      cautions: 'Persistent dry mouth with thirst and frequent urination may signal diabetes and needs medical review.',
      research: 'Porges polyvagal theory; ADA dry mouth guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_mouth_wet',
      sensation: 'mouth waters or fills with saliva',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'GI',
      zoneIndicator: 'ambiguous',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your mouth fills up with extra spit.',
        middle: 'You salivate more than usual, sometimes before food, sometimes before feeling sick.',
        high: 'Hypersalivation may precede nausea, anticipate food, or accompany parasympathetic activation.'
      },
      forWho: 'pre-meal, pre-nausea, parasympathetic-recovery',
      whatItMeans: 'Extra saliva can be appetite (good) or pre-nausea (warning). Context matters.',
      whatToDo: 'If pre-nausea, sit down and breathe slowly. If pre-meal, enjoy it as a sign appetite is online.',
      cautions: 'Sudden hypersalivation with confusion or one-sided weakness needs emergency care.',
      research: 'Mahler interoception curriculum; gastroenterology basics.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_lump_throat',
      sensation: 'lump in the throat',
      bodyRegion: 'throat',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'ambiguous',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'It feels like something is stuck in your throat.',
        middle: 'You feel a tight ball in your throat, often before crying or holding back emotion.',
        high: 'Globus sensation often reflects upper esophageal sphincter tension during suppressed emotion.'
      },
      forWho: 'emotional, grieving, suppressing tears',
      whatItMeans: 'A throat lump often signals emotion rising that is not yet expressed. The body knows before words do.',
      whatToDo: 'Sigh out loudly, hum a low note, or sip water. Allow tears if they want to come.',
      cautions: 'Persistent lump with swallowing trouble or weight loss needs medical review.',
      research: 'Khalsa interoception; globus pharyngeus ENT literature.'
    },
    {
      id: 'face_tongue_tense',
      sensation: 'tongue pressed to roof of mouth',
      bodyRegion: 'face',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 1,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your tongue is pushing hard against the roof of your mouth.',
        middle: 'You notice your tongue is held tight, often when you are concentrating or stressed.',
        high: 'Lingual muscle bracing often co-occurs with masseter clench during sustained cognitive demand.'
      },
      forWho: 'focused-on-task, anxious-holding-still',
      whatItMeans: 'A tense tongue is a hidden bracing pattern that often accompanies a clenched jaw.',
      whatToDo: 'Let your tongue rest lightly behind your lower teeth. Exhale and feel the release.',
      cautions: 'Tongue tension with speech change needs medical review.',
      research: 'Myofunctional therapy literature; Mahler interoception.'
    },
    // ===== THROAT =====
    {
      id: 'throat_thick',
      sensation: 'throat feels thick or swollen',
      bodyRegion: 'throat',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your throat feels full and tight, like it is hard to swallow.',
        middle: 'Your throat feels thick, like swallowing is harder than usual.',
        high: 'Sensation of pharyngeal thickening can accompany acute emotion, panic, or allergic response.'
      },
      forWho: 'emotional, panicked, allergic',
      whatItMeans: 'Throat thickness often signals strong emotion or anxiety. Rule out allergy if it appears with food or insect exposure.',
      whatToDo: 'Sip warm water, hum, and slow your exhale. If linked to food/sting, alert an adult immediately.',
      cautions: 'Throat swelling with breathing trouble, hives, or facial swelling is a medical emergency (anaphylaxis).',
      research: 'AAAAI anaphylaxis guidelines; Khalsa interoception research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'throat_swallow_hard',
      sensation: 'difficulty swallowing',
      bodyRegion: 'throat',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Swallowing feels harder than usual.',
        middle: 'You have to think about swallowing instead of it happening automatically.',
        high: 'Self-monitored swallowing often appears during anxiety, illness, or hyperawareness.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, OCD-prone, sore-throat',
      whatItMeans: 'Conscious swallowing usually means your body is in alert mode. Awareness has narrowed onto a normally automatic act.',
      whatToDo: 'Drink a small sip, distract briefly, and let automaticity return. Try not to grade the swallow.',
      cautions: 'True difficulty swallowing (food sticking) needs medical review.',
      research: 'Garfinkel interoceptive accuracy research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'throat_voice_quiver',
      sensation: 'voice shakes or quivers',
      bodyRegion: 'throat',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your voice shakes when you talk.',
        middle: 'When you speak, your voice wobbles even though you do not want it to.',
        high: 'Laryngeal tremor during speech reflects autonomic activation and emotional arousal.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious-speaking, emotional, exposed-in-public',
      whatItMeans: 'A quivering voice is a normal sign of nervous system activation during public moments. It is not a character flaw.',
      whatToDo: 'Pause, take one slow breath, sip water, and continue. The quiver usually softens once you keep going.',
      cautions: 'Persistent voice tremor outside of stressful contexts needs ENT/speech evaluation.',
      research: 'ASHA voice and stress literature; Porges polyvagal theory.'
    },
    {
      id: 'throat_voice_strain',
      sensation: 'voice strained or hoarse',
      bodyRegion: 'throat',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your voice sounds rough or tired.',
        middle: 'Your voice feels strained, like you have been yelling or holding back tears.',
        high: 'Vocal strain often reflects suppressed emotion, vocal overuse, or laryngeal tension.'
      },
      forWho: 'post-yelling, suppressed-emotion, sick',
      whatItMeans: 'Strain often holds emotion that was not expressed. The throat is doing extra work.',
      whatToDo: 'Hum gently, sip warm water, and rest your voice. Allow yourself to sigh.',
      cautions: 'Hoarseness lasting more than 2 weeks needs ENT review.',
      research: 'ASHA voice care guidelines.'
    },
    // ===== CHEST / HEART =====
    {
      id: 'chest_pounding',
      sensation: 'heart pounding hard and fast',
      bodyRegion: 'chest',
      system: 'cardiac',
      zoneIndicator: 'red',
      intensity: 4,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your heart is beating really hard and fast inside your chest.',
        middle: 'You can feel your heart thumping like a drum, sometimes after exercise, sometimes during fear or anger.',
        high: 'Palpitations during acute stress reflect adrenergic surge and elevated cardiac output.'
      },
      forWho: 'panicked, frightened, angry, post-exercise',
      whatItMeans: 'A pounding heart is your body preparing to act. In threat situations it is appropriate; in safe ones it may be panic or anxiety.',
      whatToDo: 'Slow your exhale (4 in, 6 out), splash cool water on face (vagal dive reflex), and remind yourself it is sensation, not danger.',
      cautions: 'Palpitations with chest pain, fainting, or one-sided weakness needs emergency care.',
      research: 'Khalsa interoception and anxiety; AHA palpitations guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'chest_racing',
      sensation: 'racing heart at rest',
      bodyRegion: 'chest',
      system: 'cardiac',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your heart is going fast even though you are sitting still.',
        middle: 'Your heart rate stays high without exercise, often from anxiety or caffeine.',
        high: 'Resting tachycardia often reflects sympathetic dominance, dehydration, or stimulant use.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, caffeinated, dehydrated, post-stress',
      whatItMeans: 'A racing heart at rest is often anxiety. It is uncomfortable but not dangerous on its own.',
      whatToDo: 'Hydrate, reduce caffeine, and use slow exhale breathing. Notice without escalating fear.',
      cautions: 'Persistent rapid heart with chest pain or fainting needs medical care.',
      research: 'Garfinkel interoception research; AHA tachycardia overview.'
    },
    {
      id: 'chest_slow',
      sensation: 'heart feels slow or weak',
      bodyRegion: 'chest',
      system: 'cardiac',
      zoneIndicator: 'blue',
      intensity: 2,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your heartbeat feels small and slow.',
        middle: 'You notice your heart beating slowly or softly, often when very calm or very tired.',
        high: 'Bradycardia perception can reflect parasympathetic dominance, deep relaxation, or athletic conditioning.'
      },
      forWho: 'relaxed, depressed, athletic, post-meditation',
      whatItMeans: 'Slow heart is often a sign of deep rest or strong cardiac fitness. In depression it can pair with low energy.',
      whatToDo: 'If calm: enjoy it. If shut down: stand up, move, and use bilateral movement.',
      cautions: 'Slow heart with dizziness or fainting needs medical evaluation.',
      research: 'Porges polyvagal theory; sports medicine bradycardia in athletes.'
    },
    {
      id: 'chest_tight',
      sensation: 'tight squeezing in chest',
      bodyRegion: 'chest',
      system: 'musculoskeletal',
      zoneIndicator: 'yellow',
      intensity: 3,
      description: {
        elementary: 'Your chest feels squeezed, like a tight hug from inside.',
        middle: 'Your chest feels tight or constricted, often during anxiety or strong emotion.',
        high: 'Chest tightness during anxiety reflects intercostal muscle bracing and shallow breathing.'
      },
      forWho: 'anxious, grieving, post-stress',
      whatItMeans: 'Tightness is your chest muscles bracing. It can feel scary but is usually muscular, not cardiac.',
      whatToDo: 'Stretch arms overhead, take 3 slow belly breaths, and roll shoulders back.',
      cautions: 'Chest tightness with pain spreading to arm/jaw, sweating, or shortness of breath needs emergency care.',
      research: 'AHA chest pain triage guidance; Khalsa interoception in anxiety.'

declarations.name: INTEROCEPTION_EXERCISES
declarations.source:
var INTEROCEPTION_EXERCISES = [
    {
      id: 'hr_basic_sensing',
      name: 'Heart Rate Sensing (Basic)',
      category: 'awareness',
      forBand: 'all',
      durationMin: 3,
      goal: 'Build basic awareness of heartbeat without measuring it.',
      steps: [
        'Sit in a comfortable chair with feet flat.',
        'Close eyes if comfortable, or rest gaze softly down.',
        'Place one hand over your heart, one on your belly.',
        'For 60 seconds, just notice if you can feel your heart at all.',
        'Notice without trying to find it harder. Some days it is loud, some days quiet.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Can I feel a heartbeat?',
        'Where in my chest do I feel it most?',
        'Is it fast, slow, or steady today?'
      ],
      cautions: 'For students with health anxiety or panic, this may increase worry. Offer hand on belly instead. Stop if it triggers anxiety.',
      research: 'Garfinkel, S. (2015) Heartbeat detection task; standard interoceptive measure.'
    },
    {
      id: 'hr_counting_advanced',
      name: 'Heart Rate Counting (Advanced)',
      category: 'advanced',
      forBand: 'high',
      durationMin: 5,
      goal: 'Measure interoceptive accuracy with internal heart counting.',
      steps: [
        'Sit quietly, no hands on chest.',
        'For 30 seconds, count heartbeats by feel only.',
        'Repeat with hands on pulse for comparison.',
        'Notice the difference between sensed and pulsed counts.',
        'Repeat over weeks and track growth.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'How close is sensed to actual?',
        'What helps me feel it more?'
      ],
      cautions: 'Can elevate health anxiety. Skip if it causes distress.',
      research: 'Schandry (1981) heartbeat counting task; Garfinkel (2015) interoceptive accuracy.'
    },
    {
      id: 'breath_observation',
      name: 'Breath Observation',
      category: 'awareness',
      forBand: 'all',
      durationMin: 3,
      goal: 'Notice natural breath without changing it.',
      steps: [
        'Sit or lie down comfortably.',
        'Do not try to breathe slower or deeper.',
        'For 2 minutes, just notice where you feel the breath most (nose, chest, belly).',
        'Notice whether breath is fast or slow today.',
        'Allow whatever pattern shows up.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Where do I feel breath most?',
        'Cool air in, warm air out?',
        'Is it shallow or full?'
      ],
      cautions: 'For students with breath anxiety, this can increase focus on breath uncomfortably. Offer alternative grounding.',
      research: 'Kabat-Zinn MBSR; Mahler interoception curriculum.'
    },
    {
      id: 'breath_length_awareness',
      name: 'Breath Length Awareness',
      category: 'labeling',
      forBand: 'middle',
      durationMin: 4,
      goal: 'Notice difference between inhale and exhale length.',
      steps: [
        'Sit comfortably.',
        'Without changing breath, count the inhale length silently.',
        'Then count the exhale length.',
        'Repeat for 5 breaths and notice which is longer.',
        'Try one round where you make the exhale longer than the inhale.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Which is longer naturally?',
        'How does it feel when exhale is longer?'
      ],
      cautions: 'Avoid if breath focus increases anxiety; use grounding instead.',
      research: 'Brown & Gerbarg coherent breathing.'
    },
    {
      id: 'body_scan_basic',
      name: 'Body Scan (Basic)',
      category: 'awareness',
      forBand: 'elementary',
      durationMin: 5,
      goal: 'Sweep attention through body parts noting sensation.',
      steps: [
        'Lie down or sit comfortably.',
        'Start at feet. Notice what your feet feel: warm, cool, tingly, nothing.',
        'Move slowly up: legs, belly, chest, arms, shoulders, neck, head.',
        'No need to fix anything. Just notice.',
        'End with three slow exhales.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Which parts had clear sensation?',
        'Which parts felt blank?'
      ],
      cautions: 'For trauma-affected students, body scan can activate. Offer eyes-open, partial scan, or skip painful regions.',
      research: 'Kabat-Zinn MBSR; Mahler interoception.'
    },
    {
      id: 'body_scan_advanced',
      name: 'Body Scan (Advanced, Detailed)',
      category: 'advanced',
      forBand: 'high',
      durationMin: 15,
      goal: 'Detailed multi-region awareness with curiosity.',
      steps: [
        'Lie down in a safe quiet place.',
        'Start at toes. Spend 30 seconds noticing each region.',
        'Sweep up through each section: feet, calves, knees, thighs, hips, low back, belly, chest, mid-back, upper back, hands, forearms, upper arms, shoulders, neck, face, scalp.',
        'For each region, note: warm/cool, soft/tense, light/heavy, tingling, ache.',
        'Do not fix; only notice with curiosity.',
        'End with whole-body awareness.',
        'Slowly open eyes.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Patterns of tension or ease?',
        'Areas blank to sensation?',
        'Surprising findings?'
      ],
      cautions: 'Trauma-affected: include grounding before, eyes-open option, and stop signal.',
      research: 'Kabat-Zinn MBSR; van der Kolk trauma-sensitive body practices.'
    },
    {
      id: 'hunger_fullness_check',
      name: 'Hunger vs Fullness Check',
      category: 'differentiation',
      forBand: 'all',
      durationMin: 3,
      goal: 'Learn to distinguish hunger, fullness, satisfaction.',
      steps: [
        'Before eating, rate hunger 0-10 (0 = stuffed, 10 = starving).',
        'Eat slowly without screens.',
        'Halfway through meal, pause and rate again.',
        'When done, rate satisfaction.',
        'Track over time.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'How does true hunger feel?',
        'How does comfortable fullness feel?'
      ],
      cautions: 'For students with eating disorders, this exercise can trigger restrictive thinking. Coordinate with care team or skip.',
      research: 'Tribole & Resch Intuitive Eating; Mahler interoception.'
    },
    {
      id: 'temperature_mapping',
      name: 'Temperature Mapping',
      category: 'awareness',
      forBand: 'middle',
      durationMin: 5,
      goal: 'Notice warm and cool zones in the body.',
      steps: [
        'Sit comfortably.',
        'Scan your body for warm spots and cool spots.',
        'Notice which areas are warmer (often core, hands).',
        'Notice which are cooler (often nose, feet).',
        'Make a body map: shade warm and cool zones differently.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Symmetric or asymmetric?',
        'Stress patterns (cold hands)?'
      ],
      cautions: 'Some students with circulation issues may find cold zones distressing; normalize and offer warming.',
      research: 'Mahler interoception; Nummenmaa (2014) bodily maps of emotions.'
    },
    {
      id: 'pulse_sensing',
      name: 'Pulse Sensing (Wrist, Neck, Ankle)',
      category: 'awareness',
      forBand: 'middle',
      durationMin: 4,
      goal: 'Practice finding pulse in multiple locations.',
      steps: [
        'Find pulse at wrist using two fingers.',
        'Move to neck (carotid, gentle pressure).',
        'Try ankle (posterior tibial).',
        'Notice which is easiest to find.',
        'Compare resting vs after light movement.'
      ],
      whatToNotice: [
        'Which pulse felt strongest?',
        'How does it change with movement?'

declarations.name: ZONE_COREGULATION
declarations.source:
var ZONE_COREGULATION = [
    {
      id: 'blue_friend_gone_quiet',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend who has gone quiet',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Stopped texting back at usual pace',
        'One-word replies in person',
        'Pulls hood up, looks down at phone',
        'Skips lunch table or sits at the edge',
        'Energy looks flat, eyes look tired'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Notice it without making a big production. Drop a low-pressure signal that you see them and you are not going anywhere.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Slow your own breath before approaching. Soften your face, lower your voice a notch, do not crowd their space.',
      whatToSay: [
        'Hey. No pressure to talk, just wanted to sit with you for a minute.',
        'I noticed you have been kind of quiet this week. I am here if you ever want to say more.',
        'I do not need you to be okay right now. I just like being around you.',
        'Want company, or want space? Either is a real answer.',
        'I am going to grab a snack, want me to grab you one too?'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'What is wrong with you lately?',
        'Cheer up, it cannot be that bad.',
        'You are bumming everyone out.',
        'Are you mad at me? (makes it about you)',
        'Just smile, you will feel better.'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Sit nearby in parallel, doing your own thing',
        'Share a small object like a snack, gum, or a meme',
        'Match their lower energy instead of forcing yours up',
        'Stay for a finite, named amount of time (\\u201cI can hang for 10 minutes\\u201d)',
        'Follow up the next day with a small check-in text',
        'Loop in a trusted adult if quiet stretches past 2 weeks'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Pepper them with questions',
        'Force eye contact',
        'Drag them to a loud social event to \\u201ccheer them up\\u201d',
        'Gossip to others about why they are quiet',
        'Ghost them because they are \\u201cno fun right now\\u201d'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they mention hopelessness, not wanting to be here, or a plan to hurt themselves, contact a trusted adult and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988).',
      yourAfterCare: 'Sitting with someone in low energy is real work. Move your body, talk to your own person, and do not carry their weight home.',
      research: 'Shanker self-regulation: co-regulation through low-arousal presence; Porges polyvagal: a calm, prosodic voice cues social engagement.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_sibling_after_divorce',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Sibling depressed after divorce',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'sibling',
      observableCues: [
        'Sleeping more than usual',
        'Stopped doing favorite activities',
        'Eating less or only junk food',
        'Snaps then collapses inward',
        'Lingers in doorways but does not speak',
        'Hides in room with door closed'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Become a stable, predictable presence. You are not the parent and you do not have to fix it. You just have to keep showing up.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw. Move slower in shared spaces. Use a quieter voice than usual.',
      whatToSay: [
        'This is a lot. You do not have to be okay with it.',
        'I am not going anywhere. Same house, same me.',
        'Want to watch something dumb together? I will pick.',
        'You can be mad at Mom and Dad and still love them. Both can be true.',
        'I miss the old normal too.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'At least you still have both parents.',
        'Get over it, lots of kids deal with this.',
        'Mom/Dad is the problem, not you.',
        'You are the man/woman of the house now.',
        'Stop being so dramatic.'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Keep small shared rituals alive (Friday pizza, Sunday show)',
        'Leave a snack outside their door without saying anything',
        'Offer parallel activity, not interrogation',
        'Tell a trusted adult what you are seeing without betraying their trust on details',
        'Protect their privacy from extended family gossip',
        'Be honest with your own feelings instead of performing okay'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Take sides between parents in front of them',
        'Make them your therapist',
        'Try to replace the missing parent',
        'Tease them for crying',
        'Promise things you cannot control (\\u201cthey will get back together\\u201d)'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they talk about not wanting to live, are giving things away, or are using substances to cope, tell a trusted adult immediately and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'You are going through the same divorce. Find your own outlet, an adult, a counselor, a coach. You cannot pour from an empty cup.',
      research: 'Wallerstein & Kelly on children of divorce; Shanker on sibling co-regulation; Porges on the safety cue of consistent prosody.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_friend_pet_grief',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend in grief over pet death',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Crying spells they cannot explain',
        'Saying \\u201cit is just a dog\\u201d while clearly devastated',
        'Avoiding the house or the pet\\u2019s room',
        'Carrying a collar or toy in their backpack',
        'Going silent when animals are mentioned'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Name the loss as real. Pet grief is disenfranchised grief, meaning society tells them it does not count. Your first job is to say it does.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Sit at their level. Slow your blink rate. Let your face show you actually care, not a polite mask.',
      whatToSay: [
        'I am so sorry. Losing a pet is losing family.',
        'Tell me about them, what were they like?',
        'There is no \\u201ctoo sad\\u201d for this. Take as long as you need.',
        'I remember when they did that thing with the sock, that was so them.',
        'You loved them so well. They knew it.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'It was just a pet.',
        'You can always get another one.',
        'At least it was not a person.',
        'They are in a better place.',
        'It has been a week, are you still sad?'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Mark the date in your phone and check in on the 1-month, 6-month',
        'Offer to look at photos with them if they want',
        'Bring a small comfort (their favorite drink, a soft snack)',
        'Help them with a small ritual if they want one (candle, drawing, planting)',
        'Be okay with silence',
        'Share your own pet-grief story if you have one, briefly'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Push them to get a new pet \\u201cto move on\\u201d',
        'Tell them what stage of grief they are in',
        'Compare losses (\\u201cmy grandma died and I am fine\\u201d)',
        'Avoid them because grief is awkward',
        'Make jokes about the pet too soon'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If grief is paired with not eating, not sleeping, or talk of joining the pet, get an adult and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Grief is contagious in a good way, it reminds you of your own losses. Let yourself feel it briefly, then do something grounding.',
      research: 'Doka on disenfranchised grief; Shanker on co-regulating low-energy states; Worden\\u2019s tasks of mourning include accepting the reality of the loss.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_friend_family_grief',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend in grief over family member',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Comes to school but seems hollow',
        'Cries unexpectedly at random triggers',
        'Cannot focus on schoolwork',
        'Wears something that belonged to the person',
        'Drops out of activities they used to love',
        'Says they are \\u201cfine\\u201d in a flat voice'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Show up consistently. Grief is a marathon, not a sprint. Your job is not to fix it, your job is to keep being there past week two when everyone else has moved on.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Quiet body, open posture, no fidgeting. Let your face be a soft witness, not a problem-solver. Breathe slowly so they can borrow it.',
      whatToSay: [
        'I am so sorry. I do not have the right words but I am here.',
        'Tell me about them, if you want. I want to know.',
        'There is no timeline for this. You do not owe anyone okay.',
        'Want company, or want quiet? I can do either.',
        'I will keep checking in. You do not have to ask.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'Everything happens for a reason.',
        'They are in a better place.',
        'At least they lived a long life.',
        'I know exactly how you feel. (you do not)',
        'You need to be strong for your family.'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Sit with them at lunch even if no words happen',
        'Bring small food (grief makes people forget to eat)',
        'Remember the person\\u2019s name and say it',
        'Mark the 1-month and 1-year in your phone',
        'Be the friend who still asks in month 3',
        'Tell a school counselor if they are not coping with basics'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Avoid them because you do not know what to say',
        'Compare to your own losses',
        'Push them to \\u201cmove on\\u201d',
        'Talk about the person in past-tense correction games',
        'Disappear after the funeral week'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they talk about wanting to be with the person who died, are giving away belongings, or stop eating/sleeping for days, tell a trusted adult and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Witnessing grief is heavy. Move your body, hug a person or pet, talk to your own trusted adult.',
      research: 'Worden\\u2019s 4 tasks of mourning; Shanker on co-regulation through presence; Porges polyvagal on the safety cue of slow prosodic voice.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_seasonal_depression',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend in seasonal depression',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Gets noticeably flatter in late fall / winter',
        'Sleeping 10+ hours and still tired',
        'Craving carbs and sweets',
        'Skipping outdoor things they used to love',
        'Talks about \\u201chating winter\\u201d more intensely than typical'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Name the pattern gently. Seasonal Affective Disorder is real and treatable. They are not weak, their brain is responding to less light.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Bring some warmth, literal and figurative. Warmer voice, slower pace, do not bring high-anxiety energy.',
      whatToSay: [
        'Winter hits you hard, huh? That is a real thing, not a personality flaw.',
        'Want to take a walk while the sun is out? Even ten minutes counts.',
        'I am going to the cafe, ride with me?',
        'Have you talked to anyone about how heavy it gets? It is treatable.',
        'I miss the summer version of you. I also like the winter one. Both are okay.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'Just go outside, you will feel better.',
        'Everyone hates winter, get over it.',
        'You are using SAD as an excuse.',
        'Have you tried being more positive?',
        'My winter is fine, why is yours not?'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Invite them to daylight activities (morning walks, lunch outside)',
        'Send them a meme or photo at the worst part of the day (mid afternoon)',
        'Suggest a light therapy lamp casually, not as a fix',
        'Keep them in the social loop even when they decline',
        'Notice if it lifts in spring (confirms SAD pattern)',
        'Gently mention talking to a doctor or counselor'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Drop them because they are no fun in winter',
        'Force them to big crowded events',
        'Diagnose them out loud',
        'Make every interaction about their depression',
        'Compare to your own \\u201cwinter blues\\u201d if yours is mild'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they talk about not being here in spring, are using substances heavily, or stop functioning, tell a trusted adult and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Low-energy seasons are contagious. Get your own light, your own movement, your own people.',
      research: 'Rosenthal on Seasonal Affective Disorder; Shanker self-reg on biological domain stressors; light therapy evidence base (Lam et al.).'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_autistic_shutdown',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Kid in dissociative shutdown (autistic friend)',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Goes completely still and quiet',
        'Stares at one spot, unresponsive',
        'May not answer their name',
        'Body looks frozen, not relaxed',
        'Often follows sensory or social overload',
        'May rock slightly or stim minimally'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Reduce input immediately. This is autistic shutdown, the nervous system has hit overload and gone offline. Do not try to talk them out.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Lower your body. Move slowly and predictably. Drop your own volume to near-whisper. Keep your own breath slow and even.',
      whatToSay: [
        'I am right here. You do not have to say anything.',
        'I am going to turn this light down, okay?',
        'No words needed. I will sit with you.',
        'When you are back, I will still be here.',
        'You are safe with me.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'Snap out of it.',
        'What is wrong, talk to me, what happened?',
        'Use your words.',
        'You are scaring me, please respond.',
        'Are you doing this for attention?'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Dim lights, turn off music, close the door',
        'Move other people away from the area',
        'Offer a known comfort item if you know one (weighted thing, hood up)',
        'Sit nearby in silence, do not touch unless they have asked you to before',
        'Tell a trusted adult who knows the person',
        'Wait. Shutdown ends on its own, often 20 to 60+ minutes'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Touch them suddenly',
        'Ask repeated questions',
        'Move them physically',
        'Mock or film them',
        'Treat it like a tantrum'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If shutdown lasts more than 2 hours, includes not breathing well, or follows a head injury, get medical help. Otherwise, follow their established support plan.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Witnessing shutdown can be scary. Talk to someone after. Learn more about autistic experience from autistic adults (ASAN, autistic creators).',
      research: 'Autistic Self Advocacy Network on shutdown vs meltdown; Porges polyvagal on dorsal vagal shutdown; Welch on \\u201cintensive interaction\\u201d (low input, high presence).'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_friend_breakup',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend after a breakup',
      forBand: 'middle',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Replaying texts and conversations',
        'Crying in bathrooms',
        'Listening to one sad song on loop',
        'Not eating or eating constantly',
        'Stalking the ex on social media',
        'Saying \\u201cI am fine\\u201d while clearly not'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Validate that this hurts in a real, physical way. Heartbreak literally activates pain centers in the brain.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Sit close but not pressuring. Open palms. Soft voice. Match their energy down, not up.',
      whatToSay: [
        'This sucks. I am sorry. You loved them.',
        'You are allowed to be wrecked. Take the time.',
        'Want to vent or want distraction? Both are valid.',
        'You will not feel like this forever, but you do not have to be over it today.',
        'I will not let you do anything embarrassing on their social. I got you.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'There are plenty of fish in the sea.',
        'You can do better.',
        'I never liked them anyway.',
        'You should be over it by now.',
        'Just get under someone else.'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Be physically present (movies, food, walks)',
        'Confiscate the phone during 2 a.m. spirals (with consent)',
        'Help them block / mute the ex if they want',
        'Bring food, water, sunlight',
        'Let them tell the same story 50 times',
        'Plan small forward-looking things (concert in a month)'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Trash-talk the ex (they may get back together)',
        'Push them to rebound',
        'Compare to your worse breakup',
        'Disappear because heartbreak is heavy',
        'Tell them what they \\u201cshould\\u201d feel'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they talk about ending their life over it, threaten the ex, or stop functioning for over 2 weeks, get an adult and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Holding heartbreak takes a toll. Step away, do something fun for yourself, do not become their only support.',
      research: 'Eisenberger on social pain sharing neural circuits with physical pain; Shanker on co-regulation in low-arousal states.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_friend_long_illness',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend going through a long illness',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Tired in a different way than sleepy',
        'Missing school, then catching up, then missing again',
        'Cancels plans last minute',
        'Goes quiet about how they actually feel',
        'Frustrated by being \\u201cbehind\\u201d',
        'May resent healthy peers without meaning to'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Show up in a way that does not require them to perform okay. Chronic illness fatigue is bone-deep, not lazy.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Bring calm energy, not pity. Sit at their level. Speak at normal pace, not slow-and-loud like they are fragile.',
      whatToSay: [
        'I do not need updates on how you are doing. I am just here.',
        'Want me to bring schoolwork, or want a screen break? Either.',
        'You are not behind. You are doing this with a harder mode on.',
        'No pressure to talk about it. Or you can vent for an hour. Up to you.',
        'I miss hanging out, in a not-pressuring way.'
      ],
      whatNotToSay: [
        'You look great! (when they feel terrible)',
        'Have you tried [random treatment]?',
        'My aunt had that, she died. (real thing people say)',
        'At least you get to stay home.',
        'You should think positive, it cures cancer.'
      ],
      whatToDo: [
        'Send low-effort texts (memes, photos, no reply needed)',
        'Visit when invited, leave when they fade',
        'Bring soft food, not flowers they have to deal with',
        'Help with logistics (notes, missed work)',
        'Include them in plans even if they cancel',
        'Learn one specific thing about their condition'
      ],
      whatNotToDo: [
        'Push them to push through',
        'Disappear because it is uncomfortable',
        'Pity-eyes everywhere',
        'Tell other people their medical business',
        'Get hurt when they cancel'
      ],
      whenToEscalate: 'If they talk about being a burden, wanting to die, or stopping treatment without doctor support, tell a trusted adult and call/text 988.',
      yourAfterCare: 'Caregiving fatigue is real even as a friend. Have your own people, your own rest, your own movement.',
      research: 'Spoon theory (Miserandino) on chronic illness energy; Shanker biological domain; co-regulation through low-arousal presence.'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_public_failure',
      forZone: 'blue',
      scenario: 'Friend after a public failure or embarrassment',
      forBand: 'all',
      forWho: 'friend',
      observableCues: [
        'Wants to disappear, hide in bathroom',
        'Replays the moment over and over',
        'Sure everyone is talking about them',
        'Quiet voice, eyes down',
        'Withdraws from social media',
        'May say \\u201cI am fine\\u201d with a tight voice'
      ],
      yourFirstStep: 'Become their pocket-sized regulator. Stay close. Project calm. Do not minimize, do not over-pity.',
      yourBodyStance: 'Casual, side-by-side, not face-to-face. Light voice, low volume. Stay grounded.',
      whatToSay: [
