      research: 'Cain ego depletion; Csikszentmihalyi flow recovery; Shanker self-reg restoration; positive psychology (Seligman).'
    }
  ];

declarations.name: ZONE_VALIDATION_PHRASES
declarations.source:
var ZONE_VALIDATION_PHRASES = [
    // ── BLUE ZONE — sadness, withdrawal, low energy ──
    {
      id: 'blue_p_that_makes_sense',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'sadness',
      phrase: 'That makes complete sense. Anyone would feel sad about this.',
      whyItWorks: 'Normalizes the feeling without dismissing it. Tells them they are not broken for hurting.',
      alternatives: [
        'Of course you feel this way. It is a sad thing.',
        'That is such a fair response to what happened.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: 'Stop saying "you should not feel that way" — it shames the feeling, the feeling does not go away, it just hides.',
      example: 'Friend got rejected from college. "That makes complete sense. Anyone would feel sad about this. You wanted it."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_loved_them',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'grief',
      phrase: 'You loved them. Of course this hurts.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the relationship as the source of grief. Honors the love. The size of the pain matches the size of the love.',
      alternatives: [
        'You loved deeply. Grief is the cost of that.',
        'The love is real. So the loss is real.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"At least they are in a better place" — religious bypass that silences grief.',
      example: 'After a friend\'s grandmother dies: "You loved her. Of course this hurts."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_no_timeline',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'grief',
      phrase: 'There is no timeline for this. You take as long as you need.',
      whyItWorks: 'Pushes back against social pressure to "move on." Grief and depression operate on their own clock.',
      alternatives: [
        'No deadline. Grief is its own weather.',
        'You do not have to be okay by any date.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"It has been X weeks, are you still sad?" — implies feelings should be over by your calendar.',
      example: 'Friend still grieving a pet 3 months later: "There is no timeline. You take as long as you need."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_just_be_here',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'sadness',
      phrase: 'I do not need you to be okay. I just like being around you.',
      whyItWorks: 'Removes the pressure to perform happiness. Says love is not conditional on mood.',
      alternatives: [
        'You do not have to be cheerful for me to want to be here.',
        'Sad version of you is still you. I am here.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Cheer up!" — makes happiness the entry fee to relationship.',
      example: 'Friend in seasonal depression: "I do not need you to be okay. I just like being around you."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_not_alone',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'isolation',
      phrase: 'You are not alone in this. I am right here.',
      whyItWorks: 'Counters the isolation that drives blue zone deeper. The most healing message in low-arousal states is presence.',
      alternatives: [
        'I am right here. You are not facing this alone.',
        'You do not have to carry this by yourself.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Everyone goes through this" — true but invalidating, makes their suffering generic.',
      example: 'Friend going through breakup: "You are not alone in this. I am right here."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_makes_sense_to_withdraw',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'withdrawal',
      phrase: 'It makes sense you want to be alone. Withdrawal is the body protecting itself.',
      whyItWorks: 'Validates the urge to hide without shaming it. Names withdrawal as protection, not pathology.',
      alternatives: [
        'Your body wants to retreat. That is fair.',
        'Of course you do not feel like socializing.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You need to push through and be social" — overrides the body\'s wisdom.',
      example: 'Friend skipping parties after a loss: "It makes sense you want to be alone. Withdrawal is the body protecting itself."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_heavy',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'depression',
      phrase: 'That is heavy. Of course you are exhausted.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names depression as weight, which it is. Validates exhaustion as a real cost.',
      alternatives: [
        'You are carrying so much. Of course you are tired.',
        'It is heavy. Your tired is real.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You sleep all the time, you cannot be that tired" — depression-tired is not sleep-tired.',
      example: 'Friend with chronic depression: "That is heavy. Of course you are exhausted."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_will_be_here',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'sadness',
      phrase: 'I will be here when you come back. I am not going anywhere.',
      whyItWorks: 'Promises constancy. The blue zone fear is "I am too much, everyone will leave." This counters it directly.',
      alternatives: [
        'I am not leaving. Come back when you are ready.',
        'My door stays open. Always.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You need to snap out of it or I cannot keep being your friend" — confirms the abandonment fear.',
      example: 'Friend withdrawn for weeks: "I will be here when you come back. I am not going anywhere."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_not_lazy',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'depression',
      phrase: 'This is not laziness. Depression is a real, exhausting condition.',
      whyItWorks: 'Directly counters the most damaging blue-zone self-talk. Names the medical reality.',
      alternatives: [
        'Depression is not a character flaw. It is a real illness.',
        'You are not lazy. Your brain is fighting you.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just get up and do something" — assumes the issue is willpower.',
      example: 'Friend can\'t get out of bed: "This is not laziness. Depression is real."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_low_bar',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'depression',
      phrase: 'You brushed your teeth today. That counts. That was hard.',
      whyItWorks: 'Honors the actual size of small tasks during depression. Teeth-brushing IS a victory when you are flat.',
      alternatives: [
        'Showering today was real work. Good job.',
        'You ate something. That matters.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You only brushed your teeth, get up and do something real" — minimizes the cost of small acts in depression.',
      example: 'Friend proud they showered: "You showered today. That counts. That was hard."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_tears_are_ok',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'sadness',
      phrase: 'You can cry. I am not uncomfortable.',
      whyItWorks: 'Removes the social shame of crying. Tells them you can hold this without flinching.',
      alternatives: [
        'Cry as long as you need. I am steady.',
        'No need to apologize for tears.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Do not cry, it will be okay" — shuts down the necessary release.',
      example: 'Friend tearing up at lunch: "You can cry. I am not uncomfortable."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_no_words',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'grief',
      phrase: 'I do not have the right words. I just wanted you to know I am here.',
      whyItWorks: 'Honest. Avoids the trap of forced platitudes. Presence is enough.',
      alternatives: [
        'I do not know what to say. I just love you.',
        'There are no right words. I am here anyway.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Everything happens for a reason" — fills the silence with a wound.',
      example: 'Friend after parent died: "I do not have the right words. I just wanted you to know I am here."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_tell_me_about_them',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'grief',
      phrase: 'Tell me about them. I want to know.',
      whyItWorks: 'Invites the deceased / lost person to stay present in conversation. Many grievers desperately want to talk about who they lost.',
      alternatives: [
        'Will you tell me a story about them?',
        'What were they like?'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Let us talk about something else, take your mind off it" — exiles the lost person from conversation.',
      example: 'After friend\'s grandfather died: "Tell me about him. I want to know."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_company_or_space',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'withdrawal',
      phrase: 'Want company, or want space? Either is a real answer.',
      whyItWorks: 'Gives them agency. Names both options as valid. Removes the social-script pressure to say "company."',
      alternatives: [
        'Stay or go, you tell me which.',
        'Do you want me here, or want to be alone? Honest answer.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"I am not leaving" — well-intentioned but can override their actual need.',
      example: 'Sitting with quiet friend: "Want company, or want space? Either is a real answer."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_not_your_fault',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'shame',
      phrase: 'This is not your fault. You did not cause it.',
      whyItWorks: 'Counters the self-blame that lives under most depression. Names responsibility honestly.',
      alternatives: [
        'You did not do this to yourself.',
        'You are not the reason this happened.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Well, if you had just..." — confirms self-blame.',
      example: 'Friend of divorced parents: "This is not your fault. You did not cause it."'
    },
    {
      id: 'blue_p_proud_of_you',
      forZone: 'blue',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'depression',
      phrase: 'I am proud of you for showing up today. Even just being here is hard right now.',
      whyItWorks: 'Honors the invisible work of being depressed in public. Most people do not know what it costs.',
      alternatives: [
        'Being here today is huge. I see it.',
        'You came. That took everything. I see it.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Why are you barely engaging?" — punishes them for the courage of showing up.',
      example: 'Friend at school after a bad week: "I am proud of you for showing up today. Even just being here is hard right now."'
    },

    // ── YELLOW ZONE — anxiety, frustration, overwhelm ──
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_makes_sense_anxious',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'It makes sense you are anxious. This is a lot.',
      whyItWorks: 'Anxiety often comes with shame for being anxious. Naming it as a reasonable response defuses the meta-anxiety.',
      alternatives: [
        'Of course you are anxious. Look at what is on your plate.',
        'Your anxiety is signaling something real.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"There is nothing to be anxious about" — gaslights the body\'s alarm.',
      example: 'Friend before big exam: "It makes sense you are anxious. This is a lot."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_brain_alarm',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'Your brain is in alarm mode. That is exhausting. You are not crazy.',
      whyItWorks: 'Externalizes anxiety as a brain process. Names the exhaustion. Removes shame.',
      alternatives: [
        'Your alarm system is firing. That is hard.',
        'Anxious brain is loud right now. You are not broken.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You are overthinking" — implies they could just stop.',
      example: 'Friend with anxiety spiral: "Your brain is in alarm mode. That is exhausting. You are not crazy."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_fair_to_be_frustrated',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'frustration',
      phrase: 'It is fair to be frustrated. That was unfair.',
      whyItWorks: 'Validates the emotion AND the situation. Many people validate the feeling but minimize the cause; this does both.',
      alternatives: [
        'You have every right to be mad about that.',
        'I would be furious too.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just let it go" — invalidates and rushes to resolution.',
      example: 'Friend after being unfairly graded: "It is fair to be frustrated. That was unfair."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_overwhelm_real',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'overwhelm',
      phrase: 'You are not weak for being overwhelmed. This would overwhelm anyone.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the universal nature of overwhelm. Strips the personal failure narrative.',
      alternatives: [
        'Anyone in your shoes would be overwhelmed.',
        'This is genuinely too much. You are not weak.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"I do not know why you cannot handle this" — adds personal failure to overwhelm.',
      example: 'Friend juggling AP classes and family illness: "You are not weak for being overwhelmed. This would overwhelm anyone."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_one_thing',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'overwhelm',
      phrase: 'You do not have to do all of it right now. What is the next one thing?',
      whyItWorks: 'Reduces the cognitive load that drives yellow-zone overwhelm. Gives a path without minimizing.',
      alternatives: [
        'One thing. That is all you have to figure out.',
        'What is one tiny next step?'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just make a list and get to work" — adds task, not relief.',
      example: 'Friend frozen with too many assignments: "You do not have to do all of it right now. What is the next one thing?"'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_body_first',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'Your body is freaking out before your brain can catch up. Let us settle the body first.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the bottom-up nature of anxiety. Tells them logic is not the first move.',
      alternatives: [
        'Body before brain. Let us breathe.',
        'Your nervous system is loud. Brain comes after.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just think positive" — top-down strategy that does not work in peak anxiety.',
      example: 'Friend hyperventilating: "Your body is freaking out before your brain can catch up. Let us settle the body first."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_makes_sense_dread',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'dread',
      phrase: 'Dread is its own kind of suffering. You are not weak for feeling it.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names anticipatory anxiety as legitimate suffering, not just "in your head."',
      alternatives: [
        'Anticipation is sometimes worse than the event. That is real.',
        'You have been carrying dread all week. That is exhausting.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just get it over with" — minimizes the suffering of waiting.',
      example: 'Friend dreading a medical procedure: "Dread is its own kind of suffering. You are not weak for feeling it."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_not_overreacting',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'You are not overreacting. Your reaction matches what your nervous system perceives.',
      whyItWorks: 'Counters the most common anxiety-shaming phrase. Names the body\'s legitimate response.',
      alternatives: [
        'You are not being dramatic. Your alarm is real.',
        'Your reaction is real, even if the threat does not match.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You are overreacting" — never useful, always shaming.',
      example: 'Friend in panic after almost-accident: "You are not overreacting. Your reaction matches what your nervous system perceives."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_safe_to_say',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'You can say the scary thing out loud. I am not going anywhere.',
      whyItWorks: 'Invites the fear without forcing it. Removes the social cost of speaking the dreaded thought.',
      alternatives: [
        'What is the worst-case fear? You can say it.',
        'Whatever it is, I can hear it.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just stop thinking about it" — pushes it underground where it gets louder.',
      example: 'Friend afraid to admit they are scared of failing: "You can say the scary thing out loud. I am not going anywhere."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_temporary',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'overwhelm',
      phrase: 'This feeling is temporary, even when it does not feel that way.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names anxiety as a wave, not a permanent state. Cognitive reframe without dismissing.',
      alternatives: [
        'Anxiety is a wave. It will crest and pass.',
        'You will not feel this loud forever.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You always say it is the worst, it never is" — invalidates the present moment.',
      example: 'Friend at peak of spiral: "This feeling is temporary, even when it does not feel that way."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_short_fuse_real',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'frustration',
      phrase: 'You have a short fuse today. That tells me something is heavy underneath.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the behavior without judgment AND points to the underlying cause. Curious, not critical.',
      alternatives: [
        'Snappy today. What is underneath?',
        'You are quick to bite right now. Anything going on?'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Why are you being such a jerk?" — attacks the symptom, ignores the cause.',
      example: 'Friend snapping at small things: "You have a short fuse today. That tells me something is heavy underneath."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_no_advice_needed',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'I am not going to fix it. I just want you to know I see it.',
      whyItWorks: 'Removes the pressure to be coached or solved. Witnessing is the medicine.',
      alternatives: [
        'I am not in fix-it mode. Just witness mode.',
        'I do not have advice. I just have presence.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Here is what you should do..." (uninvited) — turns presence into project management.',
      example: 'Friend venting: "I am not going to fix it. I just want you to know I see it."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_no_decision_now',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'overwhelm',
      phrase: 'You do not have to decide anything right now. Anxiety makes bad decisions.',
      whyItWorks: 'Buys time. Reduces the pressure to resolve. Names the wisdom of pausing in dysregulation.',
      alternatives: [
        'No decisions in panic mode. We can wait.',
        'Big decisions can wait until you are calmer.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You need to figure this out right now" — adds urgency to overwhelm.',
      example: 'Friend in spiral over college choice: "You do not have to decide anything right now. Anxiety makes bad decisions."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_proud_for_trying',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'anxiety',
      phrase: 'You are doing the hard thing even though you are scared. That is courage.',
      whyItWorks: 'Reframes anxiety-in-action as courage, not weakness. Courage is doing while afraid.',
      alternatives: [
        'Bravery is doing it while scared. You are doing it.',
        'You are scared and you are doing it. That is real courage.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You should not be scared, this is no big deal" — both dismissive and shame-inducing.',
      example: 'Friend performing despite stage fright: "You are doing the hard thing even though you are scared. That is courage."'
    },
    {
      id: 'yellow_p_water_walk_food',
      forZone: 'yellow',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'overwhelm',
      phrase: 'When did you last eat / drink / sleep? Let us start there.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the biological domain. Often anxiety is amplified by unmet basic needs. Concrete and actionable.',
      alternatives: [
        'Basics first. Food, water, walk.',
        'Body needs before brain work. What does it need?'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just push through" — overrides body signals.',
      example: 'Friend spiraling at 11pm: "When did you last eat? Let us start there."'
    },

    // ── RED ZONE — rage, panic, dissociation, crisis ──
    {
      id: 'red_p_safe_with_me',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'panic',
      phrase: 'You are safe. I am right here. This will pass.',
      whyItWorks: 'Anchors them in present safety. Most red-zone states feel permanent in the moment. Naming the passing is medicine.',
      alternatives: [
        'You are safe with me. We can ride this out.',
        'I have you. This will pass.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You need to calm down right now" — adds pressure to an already overloaded system.',
      example: 'Friend in panic attack: "You are safe. I am right here. This will pass."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_not_dying',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'panic',
      phrase: 'Your body thinks you are in danger. You are not. The panic itself cannot hurt you.',
      whyItWorks: 'Names the cognitive trick of panic. Reduces the secondary fear that the panic itself is dangerous.',
      alternatives: [
        'This is a panic attack. It feels like dying. It is not.',
        'Panic feels deadly. It is not. It will pass.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You look terrible, are you having a heart attack?" — amplifies the fear of dying.',
      example: 'Friend mid-panic: "Your body thinks you are in danger. You are not."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_borrow_my_breath',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'panic',
      phrase: 'Borrow my breath. Listen. (Breathe slowly and audibly.)',
      whyItWorks: 'Co-regulation through prosody and breath pacing. The other nervous system literally entrains to a slow calm one.',
      alternatives: [
        'Breathe with me. Out longer than in.',
        'Match my breath. We are slowing down together.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Take a deep breath" — too vague, often makes anxiety worse if done wrong (in > out).',
      example: 'Friend hyperventilating: "Borrow my breath. Listen." (audible slow exhale)'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_rage_makes_sense',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'rage',
      phrase: 'You have every right to be furious. What they did was not okay.',
      whyItWorks: 'Validates rage before any de-escalation. Rage that is denied gets bigger.',
      alternatives: [
        'Your fury is fair. That was wrong.',
        'You should be mad. I would be too.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You need to calm down before you say something you regret" — rushes past the legitimate fury.',
      example: 'Friend after betrayal: "You have every right to be furious. What they did was not okay."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_safe_to_be_mad',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'peer',
      forFeeling: 'rage',
      phrase: 'You can be this mad with me. I am not scared of you.',
      whyItWorks: 'Reduces the secondary shame of being a "scary angry person." Holds them as still loveable.',
      alternatives: [
        'I am not afraid of your anger. Be as mad as you need.',
        'You are still you, even angry. I am here.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You are scaring me, stop" — confirms the shame story.',
      example: 'Friend in rage at unfair treatment: "You can be this mad with me. I am not scared of you."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_here_now',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'dissociation',
      phrase: 'You are here. It is [day]. You are at [place]. I am [name].',
      whyItWorks: 'Anchors dissociated person in the present. Sensory and temporal grounding.',
      alternatives: [
        'It is Tuesday afternoon. We are at school. I am Sam.',
        'Right now. Here. Safe. With me.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"What is wrong with you?" — adds fear, does not anchor.',
      example: 'Friend dissociating: "You are here. It is Friday. You are in the library. I am Jamie."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_feet_floor',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'panic',
      phrase: 'Feet on the floor. Press down. Feel the ground.',
      whyItWorks: 'Sensory grounding that brings attention down into the body. Interrupts the panic loop.',
      alternatives: [
        'Press your feet down. Feel the floor.',
        'Stomp your feet. Feel the ground come up.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Just relax" — vague and impossible at peak.',
      example: 'Friend in panic: "Feet on the floor. Press down. Feel the ground."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_believe_you',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'crisis',
      phrase: 'I believe you. This is not your fault.',
      whyItWorks: 'Critical for trauma disclosures (assault, abuse). Belief is the first medicine. Most disclosers fear disbelief above all.',
      alternatives: [
        'I believe you. Every word.',
        'I believe you. None of this was your fault.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Are you sure?" — confirms the worst fear.',
      example: 'Friend disclosing assault: "I believe you. This is not your fault."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_thank_you_for_telling',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'crisis',
      phrase: 'Thank you for telling me. That took courage.',
      whyItWorks: 'Honors the act of disclosure as the brave thing it is. Especially for trauma, abuse, suicidal thoughts.',
      alternatives: [
        'Thank you for trusting me with this.',
        'It took strength to say that out loud.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"Why did not you tell me sooner?" — adds blame to disclosure.',
      example: 'Friend admitting they are suicidal: "Thank you for telling me. That took courage."'
    },
    {
      id: 'red_p_glad_you_are_here',
      forZone: 'red',
      forContext: 'general',
      forFeeling: 'suicidality',
      phrase: 'I am glad you are here. The world is better with you in it.',
      whyItWorks: 'Direct, simple, non-pressured assertion of their value. Avoids guilt-trip ("think of your family").',
      alternatives: [
        'I want you here. I am so glad you exist.',

        'Reaching out is courage. Hiding is exhaustion.'
      ],
      avoidSaying: '"You should have been able to handle this" — confirms shame.',
      example: 'Friend after seeking help: "Reaching out is the strongest thing you can do. Asking for help is not weakness."'
    }
  ];

declarations.name: CULTURAL_ZONE_ADAPTATIONS
declarations.source:
var CULTURAL_ZONE_ADAPTATIONS = [
    {
      id: 'black_american_students',
      community: 'Black American students',
      context: 'Black children in U.S. K-12 settings who carry the weight of historical trauma, persistent racial stereotyping, and disproportionate school discipline. The Zones framework can either be a tool for self-knowledge or a weapon used to police authentic emotional expression. Research consistently shows Black students are suspended at 3-4x the rate of white peers for identical behaviors (Skiba et al., 2014), and Black girls face adultification bias starting as early as age 5 (Epstein, Blake & Gonzalez, 2017).',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Sadness and exhaustion are often hidden because vulnerability has historically been unsafe in mixed-race spaces. A Black student in Blue may present as flat, withdrawn, or quietly compliant rather than openly sad. Joy DeGruy\'s Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome work names the inherited adaptation of suppressing visible grief; the survival strategy of "vacant esteem" passes through generations. Black boys in particular often face the message that crying is weakness, while Black girls may face the "Strong Black Woman" schema that suppresses Blue expression in service of being unshakable.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Code-switching means Green at school can be performative calm that costs significant energy. The student may be deeply tired from maintaining a regulated affect that doesn\'t match their internal state. True Green at home may look louder, more expressive, more embodied, and more communal. Research on code-switching demonstrates measurable cognitive load (Hewlin, 2003; McCluney et al., 2019). When teachers misread Black students\' authentic Green expression as "off-task" or "disruptive," they pathologize cultural norms.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow (frustration, silliness, worry) is often misread by white teachers as Red. The "angry Black girl" and "aggressive Black boy" stereotypes mean normal-range Yellow gets labeled as dangerous. Adultification bias means Black girls as young as 5 are seen as less innocent, less in need of nurturing, and more responsible for their own behavior. Studies show teachers spend less wait-time and offer less scaffolding to Black students showing Yellow than to white peers with identical affect (Gilliam et al., 2016).' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red Zone expression in Black students is statistically punished more severely than identical behavior in white peers. Many Black students learn to suppress Red entirely at school, which can lead to explosive expression elsewhere or chronic somatic complaints. Red is not the problem; the unequal response to Red is. Black students are more likely to be physically restrained, secluded, referred to law enforcement, and arrested for school-based incidents than peers (US Dept of Education Civil Rights Data Collection).' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Name the code-switching cost out loud. "I know being calm at school takes extra energy when home feels different. That\'s real." This validates that the student is doing emotional work most adults don\'t see.',
        'Center Black-affirming language: instead of "calm down," try "what would help your spirit right now?" or "how can we get you to a place of peace?" These framings draw on Black wisdom traditions and feel less coercive.',
        'Use Black mental health practitioners and authors in any Zones curriculum: Joy DeGruy, Thema Bryant-Davis, Resmaa Menakem (My Grandmother\'s Hands), Bessel van der Kolk in conversation with Menakem on race-based trauma.',
        'Acknowledge that the "regulation" being asked for is often regulation TO white comfort, not to the student\'s wellbeing. Be honest about that with older students; they already know it. Naming it builds trust.',
        'Build in restorative practices, not just zone-talk: circles, ancestral connection, music, movement as legitimate Yellow-to-Green strategies. Black churches, Step teams, and community drumming circles offer models of communal regulation.',
        'When a Black student is in Red, check your own assumptions before you intervene. Would you read this same behavior as dangerous from a white student? Pause for 3 seconds and notice your body before responding.',
        'Audit your discipline data quarterly. If Black students are over-represented in zone-related referrals, that is a system problem, not a student problem.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume a quiet Black student is in Green. They may be in Blue and masking, or in Yellow and suppressing to avoid the "angry" stereotype.',
        'Don\'t assume "loud" means dysregulated. AAVE and Black expressive traditions value vocal range and embodied communication.',
        'Don\'t assume that "calm body" is the goal. For many Black families, expressive emotion is healthy and culturally affirmed.',
        'Don\'t assume the student needs to learn Zones-talk in English-only ways; Black students may have rich emotional vocabulary in family-specific dialects.',
        'Don\'t assume disciplinary fairness. Audit your own Zone-related referrals by race.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'BEAM (Black Emotional and Mental Health Collective) - beam.community',
        'Joy DeGruy - Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome (book) and joydegruy.com',
        'Resmaa Menakem - My Grandmother\'s Hands (somatic abolitionism); free 5-day cultural somatics course',
        'Therapy for Black Girls (Joy Harden Bradford, PhD) podcast and provider directory'
      ],
      research: 'Bryant-Davis & Ocampo (2005) on racial trauma; DeGruy (2005) PTSS; Goff et al. (2014) on dehumanization of Black children; Epstein, Blake & Gonzalez (2017) Georgetown report on adultification of Black girls; Gilliam et al. (2016) Yale preschool implicit bias study; Skiba et al. (2014) on discipline disparities.'
    },
    {
      id: 'latino_hispanic_students',
      community: 'Latino / Hispanic / Latinx students',
      context: 'Students from Latin American heritage backgrounds in U.S. schools, spanning many national origins, languages, generations, and immigration histories. Familismo (centrality of family), respeto (respect for authority), simpatia (relational harmony), and gendered expectations like marianismo and machismo shape how zones are expressed at home vs. school. Mixed-status families face additional chronic stressors that shape baseline emotional state.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Sadness may be expressed through somatic complaints (dolor de cabeza, dolor de estomago, nervios) rather than naming the feeling. Adults may say "echale ganas" (push through) which can suppress legitimate Blue expression. The concept of "nervios" (chronic nervous distress) overlaps with what Western frameworks call depression and anxiety; it is culturally legitimate language for Blue/Yellow combined.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green at school may not match Green at home. Many Latino families value emotional warmth, physical closeness (un abrazo), and expressive joy that schools sometimes pathologize as "off-task." Familismo means students may regulate by being among family rather than alone.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Worry (preocupacion) is often deeply familial. A Latino student in Yellow may be carrying anxiety about a family member\'s job, immigration status, health, or housing. The phrase "Como esta tu familia?" is often more relevant than "How are you feeling?" because feelings are embedded in family welfare.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Boys face strong machismo pressure that channels all emotions into anger, since sadness and fear feel forbidden. Girls may be expected to be "buena" (good) and suppress Red entirely, leading to internalized distress. Counter-currents exist: contemporary Latino feminism and masculinity scholarship are reshaping these norms.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Offer zone vocabulary in Spanish: azul (triste, cansado), verde (tranquilo, bien), amarillo (preocupado, nervioso), rojo (enojado, asustado). Include bilingual feeling charts.',
        'Involve family appropriately. Familismo means many Latino students regulate by talking to mama, abuela, or tia, not to a school counselor. Frame school support as complementary to family support, not replacement.',
        'Honor that quietness in front of authority is often respeto, not Blue zone or shutdown. Asking "are you OK?" multiple times can feel disrespectful and intrusive.',
        'For boys, explicitly name that Blue and Yellow are not weakness. Counter machismo messaging directly. Cite Latino men in mental health (Eddie Martinez, Dior Vargas, Eduardo Cruz) as examples.',
        'For mixed-status families, recognize that ICE-related anxiety is a chronic Yellow background that doesn\'t go away with breathing. Be a sanctuary in the building.',
        'Use bilingual feeling charts; let students label in whichever language fits the feeling. Some feelings live in Spanish only.',
        'Recognize religious context (often Catholic) when relevant; prayer to la Virgen or a santo may be a regulation practice.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t lump all Latino students together. A 4th-generation Tejano student and a recent Venezuelan arrival have very different contexts.',
        'Don\'t assume the family doesn\'t care if they don\'t show up to school meetings. Work schedules, transportation, language access barriers, and immigration fears are real.',
        'Don\'t assume English is the home language even if the student is fluent.',
        'Don\'t pathologize physical affection, eye-contact patterns, or volume that differ from white middle-class norms.',
        'Don\'t use the word "Latinx" with families who may not use or accept it; ask preferences. Many community members prefer Latino/a/e or specific national identity.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Latinx Therapy (Adriana Alejandre) podcast and directory - latinxtherapy.com',
        'Therapy for Latinx (therapyforlatinx.com)',
        'NAMI Compartiendo Esperanza (Spanish-language mental health programming)',
        'UnidosUS - mental health resources for Latino families'
      ],
      research: 'Falicov (2014) Latino Families in Therapy; Comas-Diaz on cultural humility; Cervantes & Lechuga on biculturalism stress; Roosa et al. on familismo as protective factor.'
    },
    {
      id: 'asian_american_students',
      community: 'Asian American & Pacific Islander students',
      context: 'A vast pan-ethnic category spanning East, South, Southeast Asian, and Pacific Islander heritage. Model minority myth, somatization patterns, family honor concepts, and the post-COVID rise in anti-Asian hate shape zone expression and disclosure. NHPI (Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander) students face distinct context that is often erased when grouped under "Asian."',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue often presents as somatization: headaches, stomachaches, fatigue, sleep issues rather than verbal expression of sadness. Mental health stigma in many Asian communities means physical complaints are the safer language. Concepts like "hwabyung" (Korean culture-bound syndrome of suppressed anger producing physical symptoms) name what Western frameworks call somatic depression.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be over-performed due to model minority pressure. A student crushing it academically may appear Green while privately in Yellow or Blue. "I\'m fine" is often a face-saving phrase. The model minority myth creates a particular trap: visible suffering risks shaming the family and confirming "they\'re not really succeeding," so suffering goes underground.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Anxiety is frequently high but invisible. Test anxiety, perfectionism, and family-honor pressure create chronic Yellow that gets normalized as "just how I am." Anti-Asian hate post-COVID has added chronic vigilance for many students.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red is often deeply suppressed because anger toward elders or authority violates filial piety values. Suppressed Red may emerge as self-harm, eating disorders, or somatic illness rather than outward expression. Asian American girls and young women have among the highest suicide attempt rates of any demographic; the silence is dangerous.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Ask about body symptoms, not just feelings. "Does your stomach hurt? Is your head heavy?" often opens the door faster than "are you sad?"',
        'Recognize that disclosing distress can feel like dishonoring family. Frame help-seeking as protecting the family ("you can\'t care for your parents if you\'re not well"), not betraying it.',
        'Don\'t require students to identify which zone they\'re in publicly; offer private check-ins. Public emotional disclosure violates many cultural norms.',
        'Be careful with home-school communication; some parents may interpret a counselor call as evidence of failure. Frame in academic/wellness terms rather than mental health.',
        'Build in opportunities for Yellow expression that don\'t look like "complaining."',
        'Use Asian American mental health providers and frameworks where possible. Representation in providers reduces stigma.',
        'Recognize NHPI students separately; their cultural context and health disparities differ significantly from East Asian students.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume "they\'re doing fine" because grades are high. Academic success can mask significant suffering.',
        'Don\'t assume all Asian families are stigma-driven; second and third-generation families vary widely.',
        'Don\'t lump together very different cultures (Hmong, Korean, Indian, Filipino, Samoan, etc.) under one Zones approach.',
        'Don\'t pathologize quiet, reserved presentation as automatic Blue Zone.',
        'Don\'t assume English fluency means cultural fluency with Zones vocabulary.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Asian Mental Health Collective (asianmhc.org) - directory and resources',
        'Asian American Psychological Association (aapaonline.org)',
        'Subtle Asian Mental Health (community spaces)',
        'South Asian Mental Health Initiative & Network (SAMHIN)'
      ],
      research: 'Sue & Morishima (1982) The Mental Health of Asian Americans; Kim, Atkinson & Yang (1999) on Asian Values Scale; Leong & Lau (2001) on barriers to care; Lee et al. on Asian American adolescent suicidality.'
    },
    {
      id: 'indigenous_native_students',
      community: 'Indigenous / Native American / First Nations / Alaska Native / Native Hawaiian students',
      context: 'Indigenous students carry both individual experience and collective historical trauma from genocide, boarding schools, broken treaties, and ongoing colonization. Traditional Indigenous frameworks for emotional balance often predate and exceed Zones in sophistication. The Medicine Wheel (mental, physical, emotional, spiritual quadrants in balance) is one example of an Indigenous regulation framework. Practices must be approached with relationship and permission, not appropriation.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Grief is often communal and tied to specific losses (land, language, relatives, ancestors). Individual Blue may be inseparable from collective Blue. Healing often requires community and ceremony, not just individual coping. The concept of "soul wound" (Duran & Duran) describes intergenerational grief that individual interventions cannot fully address.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be understood as balance with self, community, land, and spirit, not just individual calm. The Medicine Wheel offers a far richer model than 4 zones. Connection to land is regulation; disconnection from land is dysregulation.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Hypervigilance from intergenerational trauma may be chronic. Adults may not name it as "anxiety" but as "carrying our ancestors." Vigilance also makes sense given ongoing experiences of racism, school discrimination, and erasure.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Anger about colonization, broken treaties, and contemporary injustice is righteous and contextual, not pathology. Don\'t pathologize legitimate political anger. Channeling anger into protection of land, language, and people has long Indigenous precedent.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'If working in or near tribal communities, partner with tribal mental health, elders, or culture-keepers. Do not appropriate practices without invitation.',
        'Acknowledge that talking circles, smudging, ceremonial practices, traditional foods, and connection to land are legitimate regulation tools that may be more powerful than Zones-talk.',
        'For urban Indigenous students disconnected from heritage, recognize that connection itself may be the healing. Urban Indian Centers often offer programming.',
        'Use We R Native, NICOA, and tribally-specific resources rather than generic curricula.',
        'Do NOT lead smudging, prayer, or ceremonial practice yourself unless you have lineage relationship; refer to community.',
        'Honor that some students may carry boarding-school trauma in family memory; school itself can be triggering.',
        'Recognize tribal sovereignty in IEPs, educational decisions, and care coordination.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume Indigenous = one culture. There are 574 federally recognized tribes in the U.S. with distinct languages and practices.',
        'Don\'t assume traditional practices are universal or that the student practices them.',
        'Don\'t adopt sacred practices as "tools" without permission and relationship.',
        'Don\'t use phrases like "spirit animal," "tribe" (as in friend group), or "powwow" casually.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to be the cultural representative for the class.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'We R Native (wernative.org) - youth-led Indigenous wellness',
        'NICOA (National Indian Council on Aging) mental health resources',
        'StrongHearts Native Helpline 1-844-7NATIVE for relationship and family violence',
        'Center for Native American Youth (cnay.org)'
      ],
      research: 'Brave Heart (1998) on historical trauma; Duran & Duran (1995) Native American Postcolonial Psychology; Walters et al. on Indigenist stress-coping model; Gone on decolonizing mental health.'
    },
    {
      id: 'refugee_immigrant_students',
      community: 'Recent immigrant and refugee students',
      context: 'Students who have arrived in the U.S. within the past 5 years, often from contexts of war, persecution, climate displacement, or extreme economic hardship. Acculturation stress, pre-migration trauma, peri-migration trauma (journey, detention, separation), and post-migration adversity layer onto everyday school challenges. Each of the three phases produces distinct emotional sequelae.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Profound Blue from loss of home, family separation, language, friends, and cultural belonging. May present as flat affect, sleep disturbance, or withdrawal that staff misread as defiance or shyness. Grief about what was left behind may not have language in either home language or English.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be rare in the first year. "Fine" often means surviving, not thriving. Performative Green helps the student blend in and avoid drawing attention.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Hypervigilance is normal and often life-preserving. Loud noises, uniformed staff, or sudden announcements can spike Yellow rapidly. ICE-related fears may be chronic for any family, regardless of actual status, given community-level threat.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge unexpectedly because the nervous system is still calibrated to survival contexts. May also appear as freeze or shutdown rather than outward anger.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Connect with a cultural broker, translator, or community liaison BEFORE any zones work. Don\'t use the student or a sibling as the translator.',
        'Recognize that direct emotion-naming may feel intrusive or unsafe in many cultures of origin.',
        'Use visual zones supports with universal symbols, low text demand.',
        'Trauma-informed first, Zones second. A student in survival mode cannot benefit from cognitive zones-talk until regulated.',
        'Connect family with refugee mental health services, mutual aid orgs, and culturally-matched providers where possible.',
        'Be patient. Acculturation takes years, not weeks.',
        'Honor the strengths the student brings: multilingualism, cross-cultural navigation, family loyalty, resilience.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the student understands U.S. school routines (bells, hall passes, raised hands).',
        'Don\'t assume the family has documentation, stable housing, or access to consistent food.',
        'Don\'t assume the student has been in school continuously; many refugee youth have had years of interrupted education.',
        'Don\'t assume what trauma the student has experienced; let them tell you if they choose.',
        'Don\'t assume English-language progress reflects internal wellbeing.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Center for Victims of Torture (cvt.org)',
        'RAICES (Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services)',
        'BRYCS (Bridging Refugee Youth and Children\'s Services)',
        'Local refugee resettlement agencies (IRC, USCRI, LIRS, etc.)'
      ],
      research: 'Lustig et al. (2004) on refugee child mental health; Suarez-Orozco on acculturation; Hodes (2000) on psychologically distressed refugee children; Fazel et al. meta-analyses on refugee child mental health.'
    },
    {
      id: 'lgbtq_students',
      community: 'LGBTQ+ students',
      context: 'Lesbian, gay, bisexual, queer, and questioning students. Minority stress (Meyer 2003) describes the chronic, additive burden of stigma, prejudice, and discrimination that shapes mental health independent of identity itself. The Trevor Project\'s annual surveys consistently show LGBTQ+ youth report higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidality than peers, driven by these external stressors not by identity.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'LGBTQ+ youth experience higher rates of depression and suicidal ideation than peers, driven by minority stress, family rejection, and bullying, not by identity itself. Blue can be deep and chronic. Affirming family acceptance dramatically reduces these risks (Ryan et al.).' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green at school may require closeting, which is exhausting. A student who appears Green may be using significant energy to mask. True Green requires safety to be authentic. Many students are out in some contexts and not others, requiring constant code-switching.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Daily vigilance about pronouns, bathrooms, locker rooms, and disclosure creates constant Yellow background. This is not anxiety disorder; this is rational response to an unsafe context. Anti-LGBTQ+ legislation in many states amplifies this baseline.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge in response to slurs, rejection, or microaggressions. The Red is often legitimate, even when school discipline frames it as the problem.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Make safety visible: pride flags, pronoun pins, GSA posters, explicit "we use chosen names here" signage.',
        'Use chosen name and pronouns consistently. This is regulation infrastructure, not a "preference."',
        'Don\'t require disclosure of identity to access support. Some students are not out and have good reasons.',
        'Trevor Project Lifeline 1-866-488-7386 or text START to 678-678 for crisis support.',
        'Recognize that "Be calm" may translate to "be invisible" for LGBTQ+ students; that\'s not regulation.',
        'Work with GSA advisors and queer staff/community members as part of any school-wide Zones implementation.',
        'Audit bullying response data; many incidents are under-reported because students don\'t trust adult response.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the family knows or is supportive. Many LGBTQ+ youth are not out at home.',
        'Don\'t out a student to parents, even with good intentions. This can endanger them.',
        'Don\'t assume identity is fixed; many youth explore.',
        'Don\'t assume bullying is the only stressor; institutional erasure (no books, no curriculum, no visible peers) also harms.',
        'Don\'t assume "it gets better" is true for every student. For some, it doesn\'t without intervention.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'The Trevor Project (thetrevorproject.org) - 1-866-488-7386, text START to 678-678',
        'GLSEN (glsen.org) - school-based LGBTQ+ resources',
        'PFLAG (pflag.org) for families',
        'Gender Spectrum (genderspectrum.org)'
      ],
      research: 'Meyer (2003) Minority Stress Model; Hatzenbuehler et al. on structural stigma and youth mental health; Russell & Fish (2016) annual review of LGBTQ youth mental health; Trevor Project National Surveys.'
    },
    {
      id: 'trans_nonbinary_students',
      community: 'Trans, non-binary, and gender-expansive students',
      context: 'Students whose gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth, including binary trans, non-binary, genderfluid, and agender students. Gender dysphoria, social transition stress, political hostility, and bathroom/locker-room navigation create distinct regulation contexts. Affirming use of name and pronouns has strong research support for reducing depression and suicidality (Russell et al., 2018).',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Dysphoria can produce deep Blue that breathing and water won\'t touch. Body-related dysphoria during puberty, menstruation, or voice change can be acutely painful. Affirming care (whether social or medical) is often the necessary intervention; coping skills alone don\'t resolve dysphoria.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green often requires gender affirmation: correct name, pronouns, clothing, bathroom access. Without these, Green is not accessible. Schools that affirm see measurable improvements in academic outcomes alongside wellbeing.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Chronic Yellow from being misgendered, navigating hostile bathrooms, anticipating slurs, and tracking which adults are safe. Anti-trans legislation in many states adds chronic political Yellow.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge when misgendered, deadnamed, or when policies feel violently restrictive (sports bans, bathroom laws). The Red is a response to real harm.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Use chosen name and pronouns immediately and consistently. Apologize and move on if you slip; don\'t make it about you.',
        'Provide gender-neutral bathroom options without forcing the student to disclose to use one.',
        'Don\'t make trans students the educators. They didn\'t consent to being a teaching moment.',
        'Trans Lifeline (peer-run) 1-877-565-8860; Trevor Project also serves trans youth.',
        'Frame dysphoria as legitimate distress that requires affirmation, not "regulation past it."',
        'Know your state\'s anti-trans legislation and how it affects your students; advocate where possible.',
        'Have a plan for substitute teachers and unfamiliar staff to know chosen name/pronouns without outing.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume parents know or support. Coordinate with student first on family communication.',
        'Don\'t assume "she/her" or "he/him" pronouns based on appearance. Ask.',
        'Don\'t assume non-binary is a phase or "in between."',
        'Don\'t require medical transition as proof of identity.',
        'Don\'t treat trans identity as a behavior problem to be regulated.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Trans Lifeline 1-877-565-8860 (peer-run, trans-staffed)',
        'Gender Spectrum (genderspectrum.org) school resources',
        'TransFamily Support Services',
        'GLSEN trans-inclusive school guides'
      ],
      research: 'Russell et al. (2018) on chosen name and mental health; Olson et al. on socially transitioned children\'s mental health; Turban et al. on gender-affirming care outcomes; Tordoff et al. on hormones and mental health.'
    },
    {
      id: 'autistic_students',
      community: 'Autistic students',
      context: 'Students on the autism spectrum, including those with co-occurring intellectual disability and those without. CRITICAL distinction: meltdowns are not tantrums; masking has real cost; shutdown is a freeze response, not just Blue Zone. Neurodiversity-affirming framing centers autistic experience and autonomy rather than compliance to neurotypical norms.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue may look like shutdown: withdrawal, monotone speech, reduced movement, inability to access language. This is a nervous system protective state, not laziness. Sensory overload is often the cause. Shutdown can last minutes, hours, or days depending on the load.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green for autistic students may look very different from neurotypical Green: stimming, special interest focus, parallel play, quiet alone time. These ARE regulation, not avoidance. Many autistic adults describe their most regulated state as actively engaged with a special interest rather than passively calm.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow can build invisibly as sensory or social load accumulates throughout the day. The autistic student often cannot self-report Yellow until they\'re close to meltdown. Interoception (sensing internal body signals) is often atypical, making zone-checking harder.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'MELTDOWN IS NOT A TANTRUM. A meltdown is an involuntary nervous system response to overload. It cannot be talked out, reasoned with, or punished out. Recovery requires sensory de-escalation and time. Shutdown is also Red-territory but presents as collapse, mutism, or freeze.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Pre-empt rather than respond. Identify sensory and demand load BEFORE meltdown by tracking patterns.',
        'Allow stimming as Green-zone regulation. Hand-flapping, rocking, vocal stims are NOT zones to fix; they prevent escalation.',
        'During meltdown: reduce demands, dim lights, lower voices, give space. Do NOT teach zones in the moment.',
        'Honor masking cost: students who appear Green at school may collapse at home. Decompression time is essential.',
        'Use visual schedules, transition warnings, and concrete language. Surprise is a yellow trigger.',
        'Co-create the zone language with the student; many autistic kids find "calm body" alienating because their regulated body is moving.',
        'Recognize that special interests are powerful regulators. Build them in.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume meltdown = behavior problem. It\'s a neurological event.',
        'Don\'t assume "use your words" works during overload. Language often goes offline first.',
        'Don\'t assume eye contact, sitting still, or matching peers\' affect indicates Green.',
        'Don\'t assume masking is healthy. It\'s associated with burnout, depression, and suicidality in autistic adults.',
        'Don\'t adopt ABA-style compliance framing of Zones. Autonomy and self-knowledge are the goals.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'ASAN (Autistic Self Advocacy Network) - autisticadvocacy.org',
        'AWN (Autistic Women & Nonbinary Network)',
        'Reframing Autism (reframingautism.org.au) - neurodiversity-affirming resources',
        'Devon Price - Unmasking Autism (book)'
      ],
      research: 'Mantzalas et al. (2022) on autistic burnout; Hull et al. (2017) on camouflaging; Pellicano et al. on autistic community priorities; Cassidy et al. on masking and suicidality; Milton on double empathy problem.'
    },
    {
      id: 'adhd_students',
      community: 'ADHD students',
      context: 'Students with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, including inattentive, hyperactive, and combined presentations. Emotional dysregulation is a core feature, not a side effect (Shaw et al.). Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria (RSD) is common. Dopamine-seeking behavior shapes zone shifts in ways that can look like behavior problems but are neurochemistry.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue can hit hard and fast after stimulant medication wears off (rebound), after dopamine peaks fade, or after rejection.
