        'Don\'t treat the kara or kirpan (ceremonial article) as a weapon.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Sikh Coalition (sikhcoalition.org) - civil rights and bullying support',
        'Kaur Foundation educational resources',
        'Jakara Movement for youth empowerment',
        'SALDEF (Sikh American Legal Defense and Education Fund)'
      ],
      research: 'Singh & Tatla on Sikh diaspora studies; Jhutti-Johal on contemporary Sikhism; Sikh Coalition annual school climate reports.'
    },
    {
      id: 'secular_spiritual_students',
      community: 'Secular / spiritual-but-not-religious students',
      context: 'Students who do not identify with organized religion but may have spiritual practice, meaning-making frameworks, or naturalistic worldviews. The fastest-growing "religious" category in U.S. youth; Pew Research shows roughly 30% of Gen Z is "religiously unaffiliated." Climate grief and existential concerns are especially salient in this group.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Meaning-making during Blue may come from nature, philosophy, art, music, or chosen community rather than religious tradition.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be supported by practices borrowed from many traditions: meditation, yoga, journaling, time in nature, creative practice.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Climate anxiety and existential concerns can produce chronic Yellow for secular youth who lack religious eschatological framing.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Anger may be channeled into activism, art, or relationships rather than religious community.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Honor non-religious identity without treating it as a deficit or as lacking values.',
        'Offer secular framings of meditation, gratitude, and mindfulness alongside religious framings.',
        'Recognize that many secular youth have deep ethical commitments (climate justice, animal welfare, social equity).',
        'Don\'t evangelize even when student is in crisis; respect their framework.',
        'Provide community alternatives: chosen family, friend groups, online communities, in-person interest groups.',
        'Honor that some secular youth come from religious families and navigate identity tension.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume secular = no values or no meaning.',
        'Don\'t assume they need to find faith to be well.',
        'Don\'t assume religious holidays are neutral; they may be loaded.',
        'Don\'t assume "spiritual" means "religious" or vice versa.',
        'Don\'t assume secular families are uncommon; nearly 30% of U.S. youth identify as "nones."'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Recovering from Religion (recoveringfromreligion.org) for those leaving faith',
        'Sunday Assembly (godless congregation) chapters',
        'Secular Therapy Project for non-religious mental health providers',
        'Greater Good Science Center (Berkeley) secular well-being research'
      ],
      research: 'Pew Research on rise of "nones"; Galen on secular psychology; Saide & Richert on religious cognition development.'
    },
    {
      id: 'poverty_food_insecure_students',
      community: 'Students experiencing poverty / food insecurity',
      context: 'Students in households experiencing economic scarcity, food insecurity, housing instability, or related material hardship. Scarcity stress is a chronic Yellow producer that affects cognition and emotion in measurable ways (Mullainathan & Shafir). Roughly 1 in 5 U.S. children live in food-insecure households at some point in the year.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue may be deep and chronic from shame, exhaustion, family stress, and lack of access to "normal kid" experiences. The student may hide poverty to avoid stigma.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green at school may depend heavily on whether the student ate breakfast. Hunger directly impacts regulation capacity.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Chronic Yellow from worry about food, rent, parents\' jobs, utility shutoffs, and surviving the next crisis. This is rational stress about real material conditions.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may be triggered by humiliation (not having required supplies, being unable to participate in paid activities, having lunch debt called out).' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Ensure food access throughout the day, not just at meals. Discreet snack access for hungry students.',
        'Audit your zones materials for hidden cost assumptions (going to a yoga class, getting a massage, going to therapy).',
        'Connect families with concrete resources: SNAP, WIC, food pantries, utility assistance, housing support.',
        'Avoid public callouts for missing supplies, fees, or paperwork.',
        'Recognize that hypervigilance about resources is adaptive, not pathological.',
        'Trauma-informed scarcity awareness: scarcity literally narrows cognitive bandwidth (Mullainathan & Shafir).'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the family is failing; poverty is structural, not personal.',
        'Don\'t assume the student has internet, quiet study space, or stable address.',
        'Don\'t assume regulation strategies that cost money or time are accessible.',
        'Don\'t assume parents don\'t care; they may be working two jobs and unable to attend meetings.',
        'Don\'t assume "they\'ll figure it out" applies; struggling kids need active connection to resources.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Feeding America (feedingamerica.org) and local food banks',
        'No Kid Hungry (nokidhungry.org) for school meal programs',
        '211 (dial 211) for local social services connection',
        'School-based McKinney-Vento liaison for homeless youth services'
      ],
      research: 'Mullainathan & Shafir on scarcity and cognitive bandwidth; Evans & Schamberg on poverty and working memory; Yoshikawa et al. on poverty and child development.'
    },
    {
      id: 'foster_care_students',
      community: 'Students in foster care',
      context: 'Students in the child welfare system, including kinship care, traditional foster, and group home placements. Disrupted attachment, frequent placement changes, and complex trauma history shape regulation patterns deeply. Foster youth face significantly elevated rates of mental health diagnoses, school instability, and adult homelessness.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Profound grief about separation from birth family, lost siblings, lost pets, lost belongings. Blue can be deep and may emerge unexpectedly around birthdays, holidays, court dates.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green at school may be performance for survival, not true regulation. Students learn to mask quickly because instability requires adaptability.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Chronic Yellow from uncertainty: When will I move again? Will I see my mom this week? Did my brother get adopted? Hypervigilance is adaptive.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge in response to attachment ruptures, perceived rejection, or sensory triggers tied to early trauma. May also present as withdrawal or compliance rather than outward Red.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Provide stable, predictable adult relationships. Continuity matters enormously.',
        'Don\'t require disclosure of foster status to peers; respect privacy.',
        'Be flexible about supplies, paperwork, and signatures; navigation is harder for foster youth.',
        'Trauma-informed first, regulation second. Build safety before zones-talk.',
        'Coordinate with the caseworker, foster parent/kinship caregiver, and any therapy team.',
        'Recognize that the student may have very legitimate distrust of "helping adults."'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the foster family situation. Many are loving; some are not.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to talk about their birth family or doesn\'t.',
        'Don\'t assume "stability" is here to stay; placement changes happen.',
        'Don\'t assume the student is acting out for attention; behavior often communicates need.',
        'Don\'t assume permission for activities; check who can sign and what permissions exist.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Foster Care to Success (fc2success.org)',
        'iFoster (ifoster.org) - resources for foster youth',
        'Casey Family Programs research and resources',
        'Local CASA (Court Appointed Special Advocate) programs'
      ],
      research: 'Perry on neurodevelopment and trauma; Schore on attachment and brain; Pecora et al. on foster youth outcomes; Greeson on natural mentoring.'
    },
    {
      id: 'homeless_students',
      community: 'Students experiencing homelessness',
      context: 'Students whose families lack fixed, regular, adequate nighttime residence. Includes shelter, doubled-up (couch surfing), motel, car, or unsheltered. McKinney-Vento protections apply: every district has a McKinney-Vento liaison; students retain right to enroll, attend, and receive transportation even without traditional documentation.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue from shame, loss of belongings, loss of stable peer group, exhaustion from disrupted sleep, and grief about housing loss.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be exceptionally hard to access when basic needs are not met. Maslow before Bloom: safety and shelter come first.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Survival mode is chronic Yellow. Where will we sleep? Will my stuff be safe? Will I get to school?' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge from accumulated distress, sensory issues from shelter environments, or in response to humiliation.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Identify and connect with your school\'s McKinney-Vento liaison; legal supports apply.',
        'Ensure consistent school attendance even when housing moves; transportation rights exist under McKinney-Vento.',
        'Discreetly provide hygiene supplies, food, and laundry access.',
        'Allow phone access; the student may need to coordinate with family throughout the day.',
        'Don\'t require permission slips or fees that present barriers.',
        'Maslow first: basic needs before zones lessons.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the family is homeless because of personal failure; structural factors dominate.',
        'Don\'t require home address verification that creates barriers to enrollment.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants peers or staff to know.',
        'Don\'t assume the family knows their McKinney-Vento rights; actively inform.',
        'Don\'t assume regulation work can happen without basic needs being met first.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'SchoolHouse Connection (schoolhouseconnection.org)',
        'National Center for Homeless Education',
        'NAEHCY (National Association for the Education of Homeless Children and Youth)',
        'School McKinney-Vento liaison (every district has one)'
      ],
      research: 'Cutuli et al. on academic outcomes of homeless youth; Masten on resilience; Aratani on health and homelessness.'
    },
    {
      id: 'children_of_incarcerated',
      community: 'Students of incarcerated parents',
      context: 'Approximately 2.7 million U.S. children have a parent in prison or jail. The stigma, attachment disruption, financial hardship, and trauma of parental incarceration shape zones experience deeply. Disenfranchised grief (grief that is not socially recognized) is a hallmark of this experience.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Profound grief that may be disenfranchised: society often expects the student to be ashamed or angry rather than sad. Missing a parent who is alive but absent is its own grief.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may require masking. Students often hide the incarceration to avoid teasing or pity.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow from visits (court, prison, jail), unpredictable contact, fear about the parent\'s safety, and shame about disclosure.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge in response to unfair stigma, comments about "your dad/mom is a criminal," or system-related disappointments (canceled visits, transfers).' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Use Sesame Street\'s "Little Children, Big Challenges: Incarceration" resources for younger kids.',
        'Don\'t require students to disclose; protect privacy aggressively.',
        'Allow phone calls or letters as legitimate regulation activity.',
        'Connect families with organizations like Children of Incarcerated Parents Partnership.',
        'Be alert to stigma in classroom materials and conversations.',
        'Recognize that some students may have lived their whole lives without the incarcerated parent home; impact varies.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the student knows why the parent is incarcerated; many families don\'t discuss it.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to visit or that they don\'t.',
        'Don\'t assume the family will be the same when the parent comes home.',
        'Don\'t assume the criminal justice system was fair to the family.',
        'Don\'t require Father\'s Day or Mother\'s Day activities that may be painful.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Sesame Street Incarceration toolkit (sesamestreet.org/toolkits/incarceration)',
        'NRCCFI (National Resource Center on Children and Families of the Incarcerated)',
        'Children of Incarcerated Parents Partnership',
        'Project Avary, Project WHAT (youth-led advocacy)'
      ],
      research: 'Wakefield & Wildeman on parental incarceration and child wellbeing; Murray & Farrington on outcomes; Arditti on family research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'multilingual_el_students',
      community: 'Multilingual / English Learner students',
      context: 'Students whose home language is not English, including those identified as English Learners and those who have exited EL status but still navigate language complexity. Emotional vocabulary often differs across languages; the languages of feeling and the language of school may not align.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue may have richer vocabulary in the home language than in English. The student might feel sadness deeply but lack the words to express it in school.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green at school requires constant translation; the cognitive load itself can shift the student toward Yellow.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow can be amplified by the chronic effort of operating in a non-native language all day. By 2pm, language fatigue is real.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge when the student feels misunderstood; lacking words in English while emotions are big is profoundly frustrating.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Allow students to label zones in their home language. Provide bilingual visuals.',
        'Honor that some feelings exist in one language and don\'t translate; let the student teach you the word.',
        'Pair with a buddy who shares the home language when possible.',
        'Reduce language demand during regulation work; use pictures, gestures, sketching.',
        'Connect families with bilingual mental health resources.',
        'Recognize that "code-switching" between languages is cognitive labor that affects regulation budget.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume English fluency means cultural fluency.',
        'Don\'t assume the family wants English-only translation; bilingual is often preferred.',
        'Don\'t assume the student speaks for the family; older students often translate for adults.',
        'Don\'t assume the home language is the dominant emotional language; some students prefer English for big feelings, some don\'t.',
        'Don\'t require parent meetings without quality interpretation.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Colorin Colorado (colorincolorado.org) - bilingual EL resources',
        'WIDA Consortium for EL standards',
        'Ethnic Media Services for community connections',
        'School ESL/EL coordinator and bilingual paraprofessionals'
      ],
      research: 'Pavlenko on emotions and bilingualism; Dewaele on multilingual emotional expression; August & Shanahan on EL learning.'
    },
    {
      id: 'gifted_2e_students',
      community: 'Gifted / Twice-Exceptional students',
      context: 'Students with cognitive giftedness and, in 2e cases, co-occurring disability (LD, ADHD, autism, anxiety). Dabrowski\'s theory of positive disintegration and overexcitabilities offers richer framing than zones alone. Asynchronous development (cognitive age ahead of emotional age) creates distinctive zones challenges.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Gifted students may experience existential Blue from a young age (death awareness, climate grief, suffering of others) that exceeds developmental expectations.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be elusive. Many gifted students have constant background processing that looks like Yellow to others but is their baseline.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Dabrowski\'s overexcitabilities (intellectual, emotional, imaginational, sensory, psychomotor) describe how gifted students may be more intense across many dimensions.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge from perfectionism, asynchronous development (intellectual age greater than emotional age), or perceived unfairness.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Validate intensity; don\'t pathologize. Overexcitabilities are not disorders.',
        'For 2e students, address both the giftedness AND the disability; one without the other misses the student.',
        'Honor the existential. Gifted kids often want real conversations about hard things.',
        'Provide intellectual peers; isolation is a Blue producer.',
        'Address perfectionism explicitly; "good enough" is a skill that gifted students often need to learn.',
        'Connect families with SENG (Supporting Emotional Needs of the Gifted) resources.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume gifted students don\'t have emotional needs.',
        'Don\'t assume high achievement means well-being.',
        'Don\'t assume 2e students are lazy because of the gap between potential and performance.',
        'Don\'t assume all gifted students were identified early; many are missed, especially BIPOC and girls.',
        'Don\'t use giftedness as a reason to deny support.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'SENG (Supporting Emotional Needs of the Gifted) - sengifted.org',
        'NAGC (National Association for Gifted Children)',
        '2e Newsletter (2enewsletter.com)',
        'Davidson Institute resources'
      ],
      research: 'Dabrowski on positive disintegration; Silverman on gifted child development; Webb et al. on misdiagnosis; Reis & Sullivan on 2e.'
    },
    {
      id: 'trauma_affected_students',
      community: 'Trauma-affected students',
      context: 'Students with histories of acute or complex trauma. Includes those with diagnosed PTSD and those with subclinical trauma effects. Window of Tolerance (Siegel) overlays Zones; nervous system protective responses don\'t fit neatly into zones-talk. ACEs research (Felitti et al.) shows the long-term physical and mental health impact of childhood adversity.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue may be dissociation (numbness, freeze, fawn responses) rather than ordinary sadness. Dissociation is a protective response, not laziness.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green requires felt safety. For trauma-affected students, the body must be safe before regulation works. Polyvagal-informed: ventral vagal activation.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow can be hyperarousal: scanning the room, startling, hypervigilance. The body is doing its job; the context is the problem.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red is often a fight response: a nervous system protective state. It is NOT bad behavior. Calling Red bad re-traumatizes.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Trauma-informed FIRST, zones second. Safety, predictability, choice, voice.',
        'Honor freeze/fawn as legitimate trauma responses; not all trauma looks like outburst.',
        'Use co-regulation before self-regulation. A calm adult body is the strategy.',
        'Avoid Restraint-Seclusion-Suspension responses to Red; these re-traumatize.',
        'Build relational safety over months and years, not minutes.',
        'Coordinate with trauma therapist if one is involved; consistent language helps.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume you know what the student\'s trauma is. You may never know.',
        'Don\'t require talking about trauma to access support.',
        'Don\'t assume the trauma is in the past; many students live with ongoing adversity.',
        'Don\'t assume zones-talk will reach a student in fight/flight/freeze; cortex is offline.',
        'Don\'t assume the student\'s family is the safe place; sometimes it isn\'t.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'National Child Traumatic Stress Network (nctsn.org)',
        'Trauma Smart curriculum',
        'Sandra Bloom\'s Sanctuary Model',
        'The Body Keeps the Score (Bessel van der Kolk)'
      ],
      research: 'Van der Kolk on developmental trauma; Perry on neurodevelopmental approach; Felitti on ACEs; Bloom on Sanctuary Model.'
    },
    {
      id: 'eating_disorder_students',
      community: 'Students with eating disorders',
      context: 'Students with anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, ARFID, OSFED, and disordered eating patterns. Body awareness work in zones can be triggering; food-related coping strategies must be approached carefully. Eating disorders have the highest mortality rate of any mental illness; early intervention matters.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue often co-occurs with restrictive eating; malnourishment causes depression. Recovery requires food, not just feeling-work.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be elusive for students whose internal monitoring is consumed by food/body thoughts. "Body neutrality" may be more accessible than "body love" or "body awareness."' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow may spike around meals, gym class, weighing, mirrors, body-revealing clothing, social media exposure. These triggers are predictable.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge around food fears, body comments, weighing, or feeling out of control. Eating disorder voice is loud and cruel.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'NEDA Helpline 1-800-931-2237; text NEDA to 741741 for crisis text line.',
        'Don\'t do body scans or extensive interoceptive zones-work without coordination with the ED treatment team.',
        'Avoid food/body-based metaphors in zones materials.',
        'Don\'t comment on weight, body, or food choices, ever.',
        'Coordinate with treatment team if student is in care; consistency matters.',
        'Don\'t schedule lessons during meal times; recognize mealtime stress.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume you can tell who has an eating disorder by looking. EDs occur across body sizes.',
        'Don\'t assume only girls have eating disorders; all genders are affected.',
        'Don\'t assume ED is about food; it\'s often about control, trauma, identity, and pain.',
        'Don\'t assume recovery is linear; lapses are part of the path.',
        'Don\'t treat ED as a phase or a choice; it has the highest mortality of any mental illness.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'NEDA (National Eating Disorders Association) - 1-800-931-2237, nationaleatingdisorders.org',
        'ANAD (National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders)',
        'Project HEAL (theprojectheal.org)',
        'F.E.A.S.T. for families'
      ],
      research: 'Lock & Le Grange on family-based treatment; Tribole & Resch on intuitive eating; Tylka on body appreciation; Schaefer on recovery memoir.'
    },
    {
      id: 'substance_use_students',
      community: 'Students with substance use',
      context: 'Students using alcohol, cannabis, vaping/nicotine, prescription misuse, or other substances. Substances artificially shift zone experience; the come-down can intensify subsequent zones. Harm reduction (meeting students where they are) is more effective than abstinence-only education in most contexts.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue can be deep post-substance-use; depressant withdrawal and shame layer onto pre-existing distress that often drove the use.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green during active use may feel artificially expanded; sober Green can feel boring or empty by contrast.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow can be intense between uses (craving, withdrawal, anxiety). Stimulants amplify Yellow during use.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red can emerge during intoxication (especially with alcohol or cannabis withdrawal) and during the come-down.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'SAMHSA Helpline 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7, English/Spanish).',
        'Use harm reduction language, not just abstinence-only.',
        'Don\'t threaten consequences as your first intervention; many students disclose only when safe.',
        'Recognize that substance use is often self-medication for untreated mental health, trauma, or pain.',
        'Coordinate with treatment team if student is in recovery; recovery community matters.',
        'Avoid food/body-based metaphors that may overlap with substance behaviors.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the student is "just experimenting"; severity varies.',
        'Don\'t assume the family knows or is supportive.',
        'Don\'t assume substances are the primary problem; often they are the coping strategy.',
        'Don\'t assume "just say no" is sufficient education.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to stop; meet them where they are.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'SAMHSA Helpline 1-800-662-4357',
        'Partnership to End Addiction (drugfree.org) for parents and youth',
        'Recovery High Schools / Collegiate Recovery Communities',
        'Alateen, Al-Anon for affected family'
      ],
      research: 'Volkow on addiction neuroscience; Marlatt on harm reduction; Wagner on adolescent substance use; Botvin on Life Skills Training.'
    },
    {
      id: 'rural_isolated_students',
      community: 'Students in rural / isolated areas',
      context: 'Students in rural communities with limited mental health infrastructure, longer distances to providers, smaller social pools, and unique cultural strengths and stressors. Telehealth has expanded but reliable broadband is still uneven. Rural youth suicide rates are notably higher than urban rates, driven by access to firearms, isolation, and limited services.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Blue can be chronic from social isolation, lack of peer diversity, and limited access to community resources. Particularly acute for LGBTQ+, BIPOC, and neurodivergent rural youth.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green may be supported by connection to land, animals, family work (farm/ranch), faith community, and small-town belonging.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Yellow about family economic stress (farm income, factory closure, opioid crisis impact) can be chronic. Geographic privacy can mean stigma travels fast.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may be amplified by limited outlets, lack of anonymity, and access to lethal means (firearms in farm settings). Higher youth suicide rates in rural areas.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Connect families with telehealth options; many rural-affirming providers now available.',
        'Honor rural strengths: independence, connection to land, family ties, faith community.',
        'Recognize that anonymity is hard; community gossip can be a barrier to help-seeking.',
        'Address means safety actively: secure firearms storage, medication lockboxes.',
        'Build connection beyond the immediate community for isolated students (online affinity groups, summer programs, pen pals).',
        'Recognize that "going to therapy" may be stigmatized; frame as coaching, consultation, support.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume rural = uneducated; many rural families value education deeply.',
        'Don\'t assume conservative politics across the board; rural communities have political diversity.',
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to leave; many love their place.',
        'Don\'t assume internet works reliably for telehealth or homework.',
        'Don\'t assume small-town support means everyone is supportive.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Rural Minds (ruralminds.org) - rural mental health advocacy',
        'NRHA (National Rural Health Association)',
        'SAMHSA rural mental health resources',
        'Farm Aid (farmaid.org) hotline for farm families'
      ],
      research: 'Hirsch on rural suicide; Smalley et al. on rural mental health; Probst on rural health disparities.'
    },
    {
      id: 'religious_queer_conflict_students',
      community: 'Students with religious + queer identities in conflict',
      context: 'Students who hold both LGBTQ+ identity and religious identity, often within families or communities that present these as incompatible. The chronic Yellow of identity tension is real and exhausting. Family acceptance research (Ryan et al.) shows acceptance dramatically reduces suicidality; rejection dramatically increases it.',
      zoneInsights: [
        { zone: 'blue', insight: 'Profound Blue from grief about loss of family/community acceptance, from internalized messaging that they are broken or sinful, and from religious trauma. Higher suicide risk.' },
        { zone: 'green', insight: 'Green requires being able to integrate or hold both identities. Affirming faith spaces and queer-affirming theology can be life-saving.' },
        { zone: 'yellow', insight: 'Chronic Yellow from monitoring: who knows what, when to disclose, where it\'s safe. Holiday gatherings, religious events, and family conversations are constant pressure points.' },
        { zone: 'red', insight: 'Red may emerge in response to religious-based rejection, conversion therapy pressure, or sermon content. The Red is rational; the harm is real.' }
      ],
      adaptations: [
        'Validate that the student does not have to choose; both identities can be authentic.',
        'Trevor Project supports faith-questioning queer youth.',
        'Connect with affirming faith communities specific to the student\'s tradition: Q Christian Fellowship, Keshet (Jewish), Muslims for Progressive Values, Sarbat (Sikh LGBT), and others.',
        'Recognize that conversion therapy is harmful and illegal in many states; report concerns.',
        'Don\'t require the student to "pick a side"; integration is a long process.',
        'Recognize religious trauma as a real category needing specialized support.'
      ],
      whatToNotAssume: [
        'Don\'t assume the student wants to leave their faith.',
        'Don\'t assume the family will reject them; some find their way to acceptance.',
        'Don\'t assume the religious community is uniform; affirming pockets exist in nearly every tradition.',
        'Don\'t treat religious identity as the obstacle; the conflict is the obstacle.',
        'Don\'t assume that "it gets better" if they just leave home; for some that increases harm.'
      ],
      helpfulResources: [
        'Trevor Project (LGBTQ+ youth, includes religious context)',
        'Q Christian Fellowship (qchristian.org)',
        'Keshet (keshetonline.org) for Jewish LGBT',
        'Reformation Project (reformationproject.org)',
        'Beloved Arise for queer youth of faith'
      ],
      research: 'Ryan et al. on family acceptance and LGBTQ+ youth outcomes; Lytle on religion and sexual minority youth; Williams Institute on conversion therapy harm.'
    }
  ];

declarations.name: ZONE_SCHEDULES
declarations.source:
var ZONE_SCHEDULES = [
    {
      id: 'standard_school_day_k2',
      name: 'Standard school day (K-2)',
      forBand: 'elementary',
